papers.title: Cognitive Maps in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

papers.title: Shifted quantum affine symmetric pairs: finite presentations and graded coideal structures
papers.abstract: Shifted quantum affine symmetric pair algebras were recently introduced as a trigonometric analogue of shifted twisted Yangians, whose truncations are expected to quantize fixed point loci in generalized affine Grassmannian slices. They are defined via a loop presentation with infinitely many generators and relations. In this paper, we consider anti-dominantly shifted quantum affine symmetric pair algebras of simply-laced split type. Our main result is a construction of a finite presentation à la Levendorskii. We apply it in type $\mathsf{A}$ to construct an embedding of a shifted quantum symmetric pair algebra into the corresponding shifted quantum affine algebra, yielding a graded coideal structure.

papers.title: Mixed Unfitted finite element approximation of band structures in photonic crystals
papers.abstract: Photonic crystals are periodic dielectric structures whose optical properties are characterized by Maxwell eigenvalue problems with discontinuous material coefficients. For arbitrarily shaped inclusions, their numerical solution remains challenging due to costly mesh generation and remeshing as the geometry changes. In this paper, we address this challenge by developing a mixed unfitted finite element method based on the Floquet-Bloch transform. Our method uses a uniform background mesh independent of the inclusion geometry, thereby avoiding interface-fitted meshing and allowing us to impose the periodic boundary condition through a direct identification of degrees of freedom. A key feature of our construction is that the resulting finite element pairs preserve the de Rham commuting relation for the shifted operator. This structure enables us to establish an inf-sup condition uniformly with respect to the cut position and, in particular, to rule out spurious modes. We further establish optimal convergence of the eigenvalues and eigenspaces, with constants independent of both the mesh size and the position of the interface. Finally, we present extensive numerical experiments in two and three dimensions to validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the robustness of the proposed method.

papers.title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
papers.abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.

papers.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

papers.title: Step-Aligned Script Generation with Verification and Recovery for Web Automation Testing
papers.abstract: Automated generation of end-to-end web tests remains costly: developers must identify stable selectors, encode multi-step workflows, attach assertions, and maintain scripts as interfaces evolve. Recent LLM-based web agents can complete natural-language tasks in a live browser session, but task completion is not the same as producing a test-ware artifact - code that is executable, replay-able from a reset state, inspectable by developers, and tied to an oracle. We present TESSARA, an adaptive test-script generation framework that converts natural-language test intent into Playwright scripts consisting of executable interaction code, goal-state assertions, and step-level provenance linking each step to its generated code fragment, selector evidence, execution outcome, and repair history. TESSARA grounds each planned step via Step-Aligned Scripting (SAS), enabling fine-grained failure localization, selective regeneration of failing suffixes, and reversibility-aware backtracking that avoids undoing likely commit points (e.g., form submissions). A three-level verification pipeline (syntactic, execution, and semantic/oracle), detects and repairs malformed code, interaction failures, and incorrect landing states. We evaluate TESSARA on three public web benchmarks, measuring script executability, oracle satisfaction, replay stability, and repair efficiency, and show substantial improvements over baselines and underlying VLMs used directly as script generators.

papers.title: On solutions to tropical Monge-Ampère equations
papers.abstract: This paper develops convex analysis on tropical varieties and investigates the properties of the tropical Monge-Ampère equations. We start by introducing notions of plurisubharmonic functions and Kähler forms on arbitrary tropical varieties. We show that many classical results of pluripotential theory extend to this setting, including an analogue of Demailly's regularization theorem. Next, we study the solutions to the tropical Monge-Ampère equations. While we establish their uniqueness, we show that the existence is not guaranteed in general. More precisely, we prove that the tropical analogue of the Calabi-Yau theorem fails for any pair $(X, θ)$ consisting of a compact tropical variety $X$ of dimension at least two satisfying a mild genericity assumption, and a tropical Kähler form $θ$ on $X$. In particular, there exist measures compactly supported in the open part of $X$ that admit no solution. In contrast, for tropical varieties that are regular in codimension one, we show the existence of solutions. Finally, via strongly faithful tropicalizations whose existence is established in this paper, we relate the tropical solutions, when they exist, to the solutions of non-Archimedean Monge-Ampère equations on Berkovich spaces.

papers.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
papers.abstract: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.

papers.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
papers.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

papers.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
papers.abstract: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.

papers.title: Negative Values of Wahl's Second Chern Number for Normal Surface Singularities
papers.abstract: We disprove Wahl's 1993 vanishing conjecture, open for more than thirty years, which asserts that $c_2^w(X)=0$ for every nonquotient normal surface singularity. Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve with a nontrivial involution having $r>0$ fixed points, and put $d=2g(C)-2$. If $d>r$, the union of the diagonal and the graph of the involution in $C\times C$ has negative definite intersection matrix and can be analytically contracted to a normal surface singularity $(X,o)$. A direct relative Chern-class computation and Wahl's residue formula give $c_2^w(X)=-r(d+r)/(d-r)$. An explicit curve of genus four gives $c_2^w(X)=-4$. Branched double covers of a fixed curve of genus two yield examples with $c_2^w(X_m)=-2m(m+1)$, so these values are unbounded below. We give the construction and intersection calculations in detail, as well as a line-bundle filtration realizing the negative value.

papers.title: Parton Fragmentation Functions
papers.abstract: This chapter provides a pedagogical and comprehensive introduction to parton fragmentation functions (FFs), the essential non-perturbative quantities in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) that describe the universal process of hadronization, the transition of quarks and gluons into observable hadrons. Formally defined as gauge-invariant matrix elements, the determination of FFs is achieved through global QCD analyses that synthesize world data from three primary processes: electron-positron annihilation, semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, and proton-proton collisions. This chapter covers the theoretical foundations of FFs, including their operator definitions and properties, the experimental probes used to constrain them, and the methodologies of modern global analyses. The discussion is extended to more advanced topics, including dihadron FFs, the three-dimensional picture of hadronization provided by spin- and transverse-momentum-dependent FFs, and the modification of fragmentation in a nuclear medium, which is key to probe their fundamental properties.

papers.title: On the minimality of the compact right-angled 120-cell
papers.abstract: We prove that a compact right-angled polytope in hyperbolic 4-space has at least 120 facets, with equality only for the right-angled 120-cell. This answers a question of Potyagailo and Vinberg. As a consequence, the right-angled 120-cell is the unique compact right-angled 4-polytope of minimal volume and f-vector.

papers.title: Hardness Amplification for Approximate Nash Equilibrium with Constantly Many Players
papers.abstract: For every fixed integer $k\ge2$ and fixed parameters $δ,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $η\in[0,1)$, we give a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from finding a $δ$-approximate Nash equilibrium ($δ$-ANE) in a $k$-player game $G$ with payoffs in $[0,1]$ to finding an $(\varepsilon,η)$-weak approximate Nash equilibrium (weak ANE) in a game $H$ with $C$ players, where $C$ depends only on $k,δ,\varepsilon,η$, independently of the action-set sizes. The constructed game is symmetric with binary payoffs. The games and strategies are represented by complete payoff tables and probabilities, with rational entries encoded in binary. Consequently, the existence of deterministic polynomial-time weak-ANE algorithms at one fixed pair of parameters $\varepsilon\in(0,1),η\in[0,1)$ for every fixed number of players would give deterministic polynomial-time $δ$-ANE algorithms at every fixed approximation parameter $δ\in(0,1)$ and number of players. Under deterministic PPAD-ETH, combining our reduction with Rubinstein's hardness result (FOCS 2016) for bimatrix games at some fixed approximation parameter $γ_0\in(0,1)$ rules out a deterministic algorithm for $(\varepsilon,η)$-weak ANE with running time $N^{O((\log N)^{1-ξ})}$ for any fixed $ξ\in(0,1)$. This holds for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $η\in[0,1)$ at a suitable constant number $C$ of players, where $N$ is the binary encoding length of the constructed game's complete payoff table.

papers.title: Engineering topological phenomena via field-driven Weyl motion
papers.abstract: We illustrate the field-driven anomalous Hall engineering via the momentum-space motion of Weyl nodes using pyrochlore iridates under a [111] magnetic field as an example. We model the system with a well-established microscopic Hamiltonian and the field effect with the spin rotation from the all-in-all-out to the ferromagnetic state. Tracking the position of Weyl nodes during the spin rotation, we demonstrate macroscopic anomalous Hall conductivity variations are fundamentally driven by Weyl node motions by comparing the full multi-band Kubo formula with the geometric Weyl node separation. The discrepancy occurs only near a critical spin rotation angle, where several Weyl nodes come into close proximity. We reveal that the evolution of anomalous Hall conductivity under the magnetic field agrees with reported experiments in an order-of-magnitude and non-monotonicity. These results elucidate the field-driven dynamics of momentum-space monopoles and provide a framework for understanding transport in strongly correlated topological materials.

papers.title: Tensorial pinching by deforming curvature cones in higher codimension mean curvature flow
papers.abstract: We develop a pinching method for mean curvature flow in higher codimension. Motivated by pinching constructions for Ricci flow, the method uses a nonlinear deformation of the second fundamental form. We introduce two tensorial curvature conditions for closed immersions in Euclidean space which extend beyond the scope of classical scalar pinching results. In dimensions at least ten, we apply the method to prove convergence to a round point under the first condition and a canonical neighborhood theorem under the second.

papers.title: Polynomial Spectral Gap Estimates for Finitely Differentiable Quasi-Periodic Schrödinger Operators
papers.abstract: We prove polynomial upper bounds on spectral gaps of quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators with small $C^{k}$ potentials and Diophantine frequencies. For sufficiently large $k$, the decay exponent is $k-34τ$, where $τ$ is the Diophantine exponent. We construct examples with lower bounds along infinitely many gap labels, showing that the leading coefficient $1$ of $k$ is asymptotically optimal. The proof uses quantitative reducibility and the Moser-Pöschel argument.

papers.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
papers.abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.

papers.title: Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit
papers.abstract: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Convex-cyclic and super convex-cyclic weighted shifts
papers.abstract: Convex-cyclic operators are considered by H. Rezaei \cite{R1}. However, there is a general lack of theoretical understanding of super convex-cyclic operators. In this paper, we analyze super convex-cyclic operators. In particular, Super Convex-cyclicity Criterion is described. Additionally, we characterize convex-cyclicity of (invertible) bilateral weighted shifts in terms of their weight sequences, which in turn correct \cite[H. Rezaei (2013) Theorem 4.2 ]{R1}. Meanwhile, we give super convex-cyclicity of (invertible) weighted shifts in the bilateral case.

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Linear Models with Clustered Outcomes: Exact Multivariate Tests and Cluster-Robust Confidence Sequences
papers.abstract: We extend anytime-valid inference for linear models from independent scalar outcomes to units that contribute a vector of dependent outcomes. We develop a parametric and a nonparametric treatment. For the Gaussian multivariate linear model with an unstructured error covariance, we derive a closed-form Bayes factor under the right-Haar prior and a matrix-normal mixture alternative and prove that it is an exact e-value at every sample size and a test martingale in the invariant filtration. To our knowledge, this Bayes factor is new in the generality considered here: a d x q coefficient matrix, nuisance regressors and an arbitrary fixed positive-definite prior precision under the right-Haar nuisance prior. It yields sequential Hotelling and MANOVA tests with exact confidence sequences. Under a common within-cluster design, the cluster-robust Wald statistic of a pooled regression is equal to Hotelling's T^2 statistic computed from the per-cluster least-squares summaries, giving an exact Gaussian benchmark with G-1 degrees of freedom. For general clustered population least-squares projections, the corresponding sandwich statistic is an asymptotic e-process, without Gaussian, common-design or linearity assumptions. Each treatment includes growth and first-order expected stopping-time results; under stronger regularity, direct comparisons of expected log evidence identify a fixed mixture precision that maximizes expected log growth through constant order within a specified family, for a specified frequentist alternative. Applied to randomized experiments with several outcomes, the robust procedure gives asymptotically anytime-valid joint tests, confidence ellipsoids and simultaneous confidence sequences for the vector of average treatment effects from ordinary least-squares estimates and cluster-robust standard errors.

papers.title: Structural stability of cylindrical transonic shocks to the three-dimensional Zeldovich-von Neumann-Döring combustion equations
papers.abstract: We address the structural stability of transonic shock solutions to the Zeldovich-von Neumann-Döring (ZND) combustion equations in a cylindrical domain under three-dimensional perturbations of the incoming supersonic flow and exit pressure. The perturbed transonic shock is completely free and its strength and position are uniquely determined by the incoming flow and the exit pressure. The solution shares the same regularity for the velocity, the pressure, the entropy and the fraction of unburned gas. The main difficulties are that the shock front is a free boundary to be determined simultaneously with the subsonic flow and the equations for all states are coupled with each other due to the combustion process. One of the key ingredients of the analysis is to reformulate the three-dimensional ZND combustion equations into a deformation-curl system and four transport equations in terms of the deformation tensor and vorticity. Another one is an elaborate decomposition of the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions so that the shock front is uniquely determined by an algebraic equation and an unusual second order differential boundary condition is obtained on the shock front for the first order nonlocal deformation-curl system, from which an oblique boundary condition can be derived after homogenizing the curl system and introducing the potential function.

papers.title: Non-existence of negative weight derivations on Jacobian algebras
papers.abstract: Let $S=\mathbb K[x_1,\cdots,x_n]$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables with positive integer weights over a field $\mathbb K$ of characteristic zero. Let $f\in S$ be a weighted homogeneous polynomial such that the Jacobian algebra $$A=\left.S \middle/ \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\cdots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right)\right.$$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb K$-vector space. We prove that $A$ has no nonzero negative weight derivation, which confirms a conjecture of the third author. An immediate consequence of this conjecture is the micro-local characterization of quasi-homogeneous singularities.

papers.title: Better Specifications, Better Code: Fine-Tuning LLMs for Behavioral Contract Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong code-generation capabilities but often struggle with functional correctness due to implicit or ambiguous behavioral requirements. We present CG2, a contract-guided code generation framework that translates natural-language tasks into structured behavioral contracts specifying interfaces, preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. CG2 fine-tunes an LLM to generate these contracts and introduces an iterative semantic validation and repair process to identify and correct incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect specifications before guiding an unchanged downstream code-generation model. We evaluate CG2 on 1,007 held-out tasks using five code LLMs: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct, Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-27B. Results show that CG2 consistently improves pass@1 over direct code generation by 1.49-3.27 percentage points (7.58%-22.45% relative improvement) and over contract guidance without fine-tuning by 1.19-2.38 percentage points (7.04%-14.65% relative improvement). Manual analysis further reveals that semantically correct contracts are associated with higher code-generation accuracy. These findings demonstrate that explicitly specifying and validating behavioral requirements can improve functional correctness without modifying downstream code-generation models.

papers.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.

papers.title: Which Immersions into Euclidean Space are Boundary Immersions?
papers.abstract: Here we study the problem of whether a given codimension one immersion $f$ of a closed and connected manifold into Euclidean space can be extended to an equidimensional immersion $F$ of some compact manifold $M$ whose restriction to the boundary parameterizes the image $S$ of $f$. Such an extension $F$ exists if and only if (i) simple conditions on orientations and wrapping numbers are satisfied and (ii) a distinguished finite subset of the first cohomology of $S$ with coefficients in a certain sheaf of finite groups contains the preferred point.

papers.title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.

papers.title: Connectivism as an Innovative Didactic Experience in Preservice Physics Teacher Education
papers.abstract: This chapter examines the use of connectivism as a pedagogical approach in preservice physics teacher education through a classroom experience conducted in a Contemporary Physics course at the Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia (UPTC). The study involved 21 preservice teachers organized into four collaborative groups. Using a qualitative approach, students selected and discussed digital learning resources, interacted through WhatsApp, and prepared collaborative reports connecting contemporary physics concepts with scientific and technological applications. The analysis considered conceptual understanding, argumentation, questioning, critical thinking, relationships among concepts, and the use of digital resources. Students' reports and feedback indicated favorable perceptions of the collaborative activities and provided examples of conceptual connections, evidence-based explanations, and reflection on future teaching practices. The chapter discusses the possibilities of connectivist learning networks for physics teacher education, drawing on the findings of this particular classroom experience.

papers.title: Tilting theory on continuous quivers (I) maximal rigid and tilting subcategories
papers.abstract: Let $\mathrm{rep}(\mathbb I)$ be the category of finitely generated persistence modules on the interval $\mathbb I\subseteq\mathbb R$. We study the maximal rigid subcategories of $\mathrm{rep}(\mathbb I)$. Maximal rigid interval consistent subcategories are classified via tilting modules over the corresponding discrete type $A$ quiver. We compare several related notions, (weak) tilting and maximal rigidity, in both the context of hereditary abelian categories with enough projective objects and $\mathrm{rep}(\mathbb I)$ and prove that every maximal rigid interval consistent subcategory is weak tilting and every maximal rigid consistent below subcategory is tilting. We also establish a continuous analogue of Ingalls-Thomas's bijection by showing a bijection between integrally supported maximal rigid consistent below subcategories and integrally generated torsion classes.

papers.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.

papers.title: Recurrent Vision Transformers for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation Under Slow Relative Motions
papers.abstract: Vision-based object pose estimation is vital for conducting spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO). Recent research has demonstrated the robustness of event cameras against the harsh lighting conditions that often occur in orbit, thanks to the extremely high dynamic range of event sensors. However, event-based spacecraft pose estimation (EBSPE) suffers when the relative motion between the chaser and target is slow, since the event rate drops significantly, leading to data with low signal-to-noise ratio. Unfortunately, for safety reasons, real RPO trajectories often involve slow relative motions (e.g., down to 1 mm/s), and operating under low illumination exacerbates the problem. Addressing slow relative motions is thus crucial to raise the practicality of EBSPE. To this end, we propose using recurrent vision transformers (RVT) for EBSPE. The key idea is to exploit recurrent memory to capture longer-term information across sparse event streams, and to learn the temporal attention span from full trajectories rather than fixing the time window. We developed an RVT-based heatmap regressor to produce 2D-3D correspondences for pose estimation, which was validated on real event data collected under slow relative motions representative of RPO trajectories. Results indicate the superior pose estimation accuracy and stability of our RVT-based method, relative to previous per-event-frame-based or fixed-time-window EBSPE methods.

papers.title: High Precision Multiplicative-Error Approximation of $\#$SAC$^1$ Functions in Logspace Uniform AC$^1$
papers.abstract: Cheng and Wang (CCC' 24) showed that BPL is contained in logspace uniform AC$^1$ (denoted as L-AC$^1$). We upgrade their result by showing that approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions can be computed in L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Previously, approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions are known to be in $\mathsf{NC}^2$ via its exact computation given by Vinay (CCC' 91). A main corollary of our result is that Probabilisitic polynomial time logspace AuxPDMs and Read-$k$ logspace PTMs are computable by L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Notice that multiplicative error approximations are stronger than additive error approximations in the sense that they can be used to decide both non-deterministic computations and two-sided error probabilistic computations. We note that recently OpenAI announced that BPL $=$ L. Even if we only consider derandomizing probabilistic logspace, our L-AC$^1$ computation has the advantage that the error can be $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$ and can be multiplicative.

papers.title: Quantum symmetric spaces at roots of 1
papers.abstract: We study the integral form of quantized coordinate algebras of symmetric spaces and its specializations at roots of unity. Our main tool is an integral localization, whose classical specialization recovers the open Borel orbit in the symmetric space. At a suitable odd root of unity, we prove that the quantum symmetric space is a finite projective module over its Frobenius center, which is canonically isomorphic to the classical coordinate algebra of the symmetric space. We show that the fibre algebras are isomorphic along each double Bruhat cell of the symmetric space. We determine the PI degree and propose a conjectural dimension formula for irreducible modules. In the simply connected case, we introduce a framed Kac-Moody data, which leads to a description of fibre algebras of quantum symmetric spaces via those of quantum Schubert cells.

papers.title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

papers.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.

papers.title: Conditional Average Treatment Effect Distillation for Hypothetical State-Intervention Targeting Under Budget Constraints
papers.abstract: Personalized public-health targeting must capture heterogeneous intervention benefits while remaining interpretable under resource constraints. Flexible causal-effect models can be hard to operationalize, while coarse subgroup policies may lose individualized effect information. We study budget-constrained hypothetical state interventions in observational data without a logged historical decision policy. For obesity, elevated glucose, and lifetime smoking-history states, causal-structure-informed pretreatment covariates are prespecified, with capacity capped at 70% of those observed in the adverse state. We evaluate causal distillation where Causal Forest and Bayesian Causal Forest teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which decision tree and random forest students approximate. We compare individualized policies with unsupervised K-means subgroup policies and supervised causal-tree policies with leaf counts matched to K-means cluster counts. Observational policies are assessed on held-out data using a doubly robust estimator, bootstrap uncertainty, and decision-focused teacher-student fidelity measures. Across PIMA obesity and glucose and NHANES smoking-history experiments, each distilled student was within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738-0.937. K-means and causal-tree policies were also competitive, with the highest point-estimate policy varying by application. Prespecified paired comparisons were nonsignificant after Holm adjustment, while near-budget-boundary agreement was less stable than global fidelity for some teacher-student pairs. Findings support causal distillation for translating flexible effect models into simpler budgeted targeting rules, although observational estimates depend on causal-identification assumptions and require longitudinal or prospective validation.

papers.title: Humanoid SRL: Augmenting Humanoids with Supernumerary Limbs for Coordinated Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are envisioned to perform diverse human-level tasks through their anthropomorphic morphology. Their dual-arm configuration enables a broad range of everyday actions. Yet, as in humans, this morphology can constrain loco-manipulation when both arms are occupied or additional contacts are required beyond their reach. Supernumerary robotic limbs (SRLs) offer a way to extend these capabilities, but their integration requires the added limb to be coordinated with whole-body motion and balance. In this study, we develop and integrate a supernumerary arm into a humanoid platform to investigate how morphological augmentation reshapes its feasible action space. Through quantitative analysis and hardware experiments across two configurations, we show how the additional limb expands whole-body interaction capabilities by enabling manipulation and support to be coordinated beyond the constraints of the native dual-arm configuration. To control this augmented morphology, we leverage model-based trajectory optimization (TO) to generate dynamically feasible motions for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) controllers. The controllers are trained in simulation and transferred to hardware in a zero-shot manner, enabling coordinated whole-body skills for contact-rich tri-arm loco-manipulation. We further show vision-guided autonomous execution on selected tasks using diffusion policies trained from hardware demonstrations. Our findings suggest that humanoid morphology need not be restricted to human-like forms, but can be reimagined as an extensible design space for robotic augmentation.

papers.title: Selecting and Composing Agent Design Patterns: Industrial Case Evidence and Controlled Reference-System Experiments
papers.abstract: Agent pattern catalogs describe architectural alternatives, but engineers also need evidence for selecting and composing them. We extend a cognitive-function--execution-topology framework with an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. The study combines two industrial case accounts, a contributor's collaboration design, seven practitioner workshops, and executable fault-injection experiments. Three local reference systems use SQLite state, shared artifact files, and a file-backed map-publication surrogate. A 2 x 2 ablation separates function-specific contracts from execution controls across 36 scenario families, with ten input variants per family. Under equal family weighting, composition correctly completes or safely refuses 11 of 12 families in each system, compared with 2, 2, and 1 for the simple baselines. These are constructed challenge-suite results, not production success rates. Recovery without consumer-side verification increases false-success cases in the map surrogate. All composed systems still fail a boundary case in which trusted evidence is wrong. An audit of a frozen six-arm language-model pilot reproduces its scores but confirms an evaluator-dependent ranking reversal. The contribution connects industrial failure, pattern selection, executable treatment, external acceptance, and revision. Selection is demonstrated rather than evaluated against an alternative procedure; catalog admission rests on separate criteria. The results support bounded composition mechanisms, not a claim that the framework improves engineers' design decisions over an equally informative conventional method.

papers.title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering
papers.abstract: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.

papers.title: Where Do the Gaussians Go? Foreground Attraction for Camera-Based Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy
papers.abstract: Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy models can be trained without 3D labels by rendering their predictions into the images and supervising them with 2D pseudo labels. In sparse Gaussian representations trained this way, Gaussian positions are learned only through pixel-wise rendering losses, which we hypothesize give small foreground objects little weight. In trained GaussianFlowOcc models, the Gaussian density on foreground voxels is on average only 1.62 times that on background voxels. We propose a training-only foreground attraction loss that back-projects foreground pseudo-label pixels with pseudo depth and pulls nearby Gaussians toward these 3D points, favoring Gaussians that already predict the target class; the inference network is unchanged. On Occ3D-nuScenes, the loss raises this concentration to 2.40 over three seeds. Over three seeds, the mean foreground IoU increases from 6.29 to 6.96 and is higher for each seed, whereas the change in mean mIoU (13.53 to 13.82) is within the seed-to-seed variation of the baseline. Single-run ablations further indicate that pseudo-label targets outperform targets placed at ground-truth voxels and that acting on the Gaussian positions alone is not sufficient, and a single-seed test shows that the model degrades less when fewer Gaussians are kept at inference.

papers.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
papers.abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.

papers.title: Confidence-Guided Pseudo-Label Refinement for Unsupervised Cross-Domain Person Re-Identification
papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-domain person re-identification remains challenging because domain shifts generate noisy pseudo labels that are reinforced during iterative adaptation. Existing clustering-based methods often rely on limited reliability cues or global confidence criteria and may impose hard identity supervision on ambiguous target samples. To address these limitations, we propose CGPLR, a confidence-guided pseudo-label refinement framework for unsupervised domain-adaptive person re-identification. CGPLR estimates sample-level reliability by jointly modeling centroid compatibility, local neighborhood consistency, separation from the strongest competing cluster and temporal assignment stability. The resulting confidence distribution is used to derive cluster-adaptive upper and lower thresholds for a three-way selective decision. Reliable assignments are preserved, recoverable samples are reassigned only when an alternative cluster receives sufficient geometric and neighborhood support and highly ambiguous samples are deferred from hard identity supervision. The learning objective adapts to these decisions through confidence-weighted supervision for preserved samples, cautious corrected-label weighting for reassigned samples and label-free representation consistency for deferred samples. CGPLR achieves 76.4% Rank-1 accuracy and 47.6% mean average precision (mAP) on Market-1501 to MSMT17, and 95.1% Rank-1 accuracy and 87.7% mAP on MSMT17 to Market-1501, demonstrating effective reliability-aware selective adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/Sundas058/CGPLR.

papers.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Gated SHAP-Dirichlet Refinement for MRI-Based Depression Classification
papers.abstract: Structural MRI-based classification of major depressive disorder (MDD) remains challenging due to subtle, heterogeneous anatomical changes. We propose uncertainty-gated SHAP-Dirichlet refinement, a post-hoc reliability layer that improves predictions without retraining the classifier. The method retrieves similar labeled SHAP explanations, constructs Dirichlet class evidence, and selectively refines uncertain predictions through probabilistic fusion, while allowing unreliable cases to be deferred for expert review. We evaluate five classifiers on 504 SRPBS subjects (252 controls and 252 MDD patients) using 159 anatomical features and repeated nested cross-validation. Refinement improved accuracy across all 8 repetitions for TabM and ResNet, yielding mean gains of 1.04 and 0.45 percentage points (sign test p=0.008), while modifying at most 8.3% of predictions. Gains were concentrated among low-confidence cases, with significant improvements in calibration. The method also benefited an RBF support vector machine but not logistic regression or random forests. Ablations confirmed the importance of uncertainty gating and soft fusion. Dirichlet evidence identified baseline errors (AUROC 0.62), while deferring 50% of cases increased retained-case accuracy to approximately 75%. These findings support selective explanation-guided refinement as a practical approach to improving prediction reliability and facilitating expert triage in MDD classification.

papers.title: Formalization of Rényi Differential Privacy in Isabelle/HOL (Draft version)
papers.abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a gold-standard definition of privacy designed to evaluate the privacy guarantee of databases. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is an important variant of DP that gives tight evaluations of machine learning algorithms. These formulations are easy to understand, but evaluating privacy for actual databases is complicated. Even a small change in the database can break its privacy, and evaluations of DP and RDP themselves are complicated. In particular, RDP evaluations in recent studies have become much harder. Therefore, formal verification of them has been studied for over a decade. In this paper, we propose an Isabelle/HOL library for formalizing Rényi differential privacy in a general setting. We first formalize RDP for continuous distributions. As a technical basis, we formalize several properties of convex functions and $f$-divergences for nonnegative convex functions. We formalize basic properties of RDP, conversion laws from RDP to DP, the moment accountants in DP, and the Gaussian mechanism and its RDP. Finally, we discuss the stochastic gradient descent mechanism with Gaussian noise and formalize a rough evaluation of its RDP and DP.

papers.title: TNVD-SC: Diagnosing Scan Context Failures in Forests with Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distributions
papers.abstract: Long-term LiDAR place recognition in forests is difficult because repetitive vegetation and uneven terrain create severe structural aliasing. We diagnose Scan Context (SC) by separating candidate retrieval from fine matching: on the standardized TreeLoc++ Wild-Places protocol, a TNVD support key places a valid location in the top-25 set for approximately 99% of queries, while conventional SC matching on those candidates reaches only 61.84% mean R@1. With an identical raw-SC candidate set, terrain normalization improves max-height cells by only 1.21 points but vertical-distribution cells by 19.72 points. These observations motivate Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distribution Scan Context (TNVD-SC), which preserves the SC ring-sector topology while encoding terrain-relative vertical probability distributions. Under the standardized TreeLoc++ protocol, TNVD-SC reaches 91.83% mean R@1 and attains the highest R@1 mean and R@1 stability among the compared methods, while TreeLoc++ remains stronger in mean MR, MF1, and AUC. The unchanged method reaches 85.14% mean R@1 on the four-session CVTNet-style NCLT evaluation. A lossless count-coded implementation with exact hierarchical Jensen-Shannon search reduces descriptor payload by 3.86x and compute latency by 23.8% without changing the audited retrieval outputs.

papers.title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
papers.abstract: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Robust Monitoring of Dense-Time Temporal Logic
papers.abstract: Motivated by the use of third-party testing, this paper presents a privacy-preserving implementation of the robustness monitoring of Signal Temporal Logic (STL). STL is a specification language for systems whose output traces have real-valued timestamps -- most prominently, cyber-physical systems. Its robust semantics, which assign real rather than binary truth values, are an essential ingredient of systems testing and runtime monitoring. In a number of system testing scenarios, the designer and the tester are separate parties. This testing-as-a-service model is common in software, avionics, and semiconductors, and is growing in importance in the red-teaming of machine learning models. In such a model, the designer seeks to preserve the privacy (or secrecy) of its design, while the tester seeks to preserve the privacy of its collateral, including the detailed specification suite. This paper presents a secure multi-party implementation of the robust semantics using arithmetic circuits. This implementation allows one party, which provides a secret trace, and a second party which provides a secret formula, to jointly compute the robustness without either party being able to learn the other party's secret input. We present a number of algorithmic modifications to the robustness computation to enable an efficient multi-party robustness computation. We also present new, semi-linear, robust semantics for STL that take advantage of the efficiencies of arithmetic circuits. The experimental results demonstrate that not only is this privacy-preserving monitor efficient on its own, but also that it can be used in a testing loop without affecting the speed at which bugs are found during robustness-guided system testing.

papers.title: Think, Compress, Answer: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Grounding via Reasoning Compression
papers.abstract: Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.

papers.title: Visual Memory and Textual Alignment for Cross-Modal Few-Shot Segmentation
papers.abstract: Few-shot segmentation (FSS) aims to segment target objects with limited annotated examples. Recent studies have begun to explore large foundation models to improve generalization for this task. In particular, SAM 3 provides strong visual representations and supports text-guided segmentation. However, its performance remains limited in specialized domains, where semantic prompts and visual representations are often poorly aligned. To address this challenge, we propose ViTA-SAM, a framework built upon SAM 3 that integrates visual memory and textual features through cross-modal alignment. Specifically, we construct a visual memory module that encodes support features together with their corresponding masks, providing support-aware visual guidance for query prediction. In parallel, we leverage the text encoder of SAM 3 to extract semantic features as complementary priors. To bridge the gap between semantic and visual representations, we introduce a cross-modal alignment module that conditions textual features on memory-enhanced visual representations, yielding more consistent and visually grounded predictions. In addition, we propose a pseudo-label refinement strategy that updates the memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive representation learning. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ViTA-SAM achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods, outperforming the strongest competing method by over 5% in average mIoU.

papers.title: Cohomology and Representation Theory for Lie Superalgebras
papers.abstract: In this paper the authors describe two general frameworks for studying algebraic supergroup and Lie superalgebra representations. These encompass the well-known rational representations for a reductive algebraic group and the parabolic Category ${\mathcal O}$ for semisimple Lie algebras. Many of the important developments will be surveyed and a blueprint for these new approaches will be provided. The existence of odd elements simply add an additional layer of difficulty. The authors prove that the calculation of the sheaf cohomology in the super setting for the rational category is equivalent to understanding the Lie superalgebra cohomology. This generalizes the well-known fact that the classical Bott-Borel-Weil theorem is equivalent to Kostant's theorem. Furthermore, for the parabolic Category ${\mathcal O}^{\mathfrak p}$ where ${\mathfrak p}$ is a principal parabolic, the authors show that the characters of simple modules can be obtained by looking at natural generalizations of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials given by extensions between simple modules and costandard modules arising from the underlying costandardly stratified category.

papers.title: Sampling of Signals on Multigraphs: From Removable and Uniqueness sets to Spectral Proxies
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the sampling of bandlimited signals on multigraphs, where several graphs with different shift operators are defined on the same set of nodes. Since the shift operators do not commute in general, they admit only a joint block diagonalization, and the frequencies of the multigraph signal model are matrices rather than scalars. Relying on a formal algebraic convolutional signal model, we introduce a notion of frequency and bandwidth for multigraph signals that does not depend on any individual layer, and we extend the notions of removable and uniqueness sets to multigraphs. We prove that the optimality of a sampling set is determined exclusively by the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces, and not by any individual layer, although the individual layers provide computable sufficient conditions that certify a sampling set as a uniqueness set. Since identifying which layers provide reliable certificates requires spectral information, we propose an aggregate operator that pools the information of all the layers, is computable directly from the shift operators, and certifies uniqueness without any assumption on the individual layers. This operator leads to a greedy sampling algorithm that does not require computing the joint block diagonalization. Numerical experiments on multigraphs whose layers order the frequencies inconsistently show that the proposed algorithm selects better-conditioned sampling sets and attains lower reconstruction errors than single-layer methods.

papers.title: PMR-Aided Shifted-Pruning SCL-Flip Decoding for CRC-Aided Polar Codes
papers.abstract: We propose a posterior-mass rescue (PMR)-aided shifted-pruning SCL-flip decoder for CRC-aided polar codes. After CRC-aided SCL (CA-SCL) and differential-metric shifted-pruning recovery fail to find a CRC-valid candidate, PMR locally continues discarded prefixes stored during the initial CA-SCL pass, ranked by estimated posterior mass, without increasing the shifted-pruning retry budget. Simulation results for a (128, 64) code with the Reed-Muller (RM) rate profile and a (256, 128) code with the polarization-weight (PW) rate profile, both using an 11-bit CRC, show lower observed FER than SCLF-Diff (T = 15) and the considered literature baselines under the evaluated recovery budgets, with observed FER close to that of SCLF-Diff (T = 20). At the reported moderate and high SNRs, the average reconstruction-aware path-step count is within a few percent of that of SCLF-Diff (T = 20), while at 2.0 dB it is 9.4% and 4.3% higher for the two codes, respectively. The proposed decoder also has a larger worst-case path-step bound.

papers.title: Negation without Confusion: Decomposing Bias and Recomposing Style in Text Embeddings for Negation-aware Image Generation
papers.abstract: Negation-aware image generation remains challenging for text-to-image diffusion models, which often struggle with negation due to implicit linguistic biases that are deeply entangled within text representations. As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of Decompose and Recompose text embedding (Dero), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, Dero realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, Dero can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores.

papers.title: Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners: Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere
papers.abstract: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.

papers.title: Deformability of neutron-deficient Sn nuclei studied with semi-realistic interaction
papers.abstract: Although Sn nuclei have long been considered typical spherical nuclei, the $E2$ transitions in neutron-deficient Sn nuclei have posed a puzzle. We argue that their deformability may resolve this issue, based on self-consistent calculations with a semi-realistic interaction. The significant role of the pseudo-spin symmetry, which is attributed to the effects of the tensor force, is also discussed.

papers.title: Saga: an in silico ontology for a multimodal patient world model
papers.abstract: Simulating an individual's disease course requires connecting patient history to future events, clinical timing and disease morphology.
