We represent each motor development scale as a developmental graph that guides the training of a humanoid robot. We then apply this graph within a reinforcement learning framework so that the robot learns skills following the natural phases of human motor development described by the scale. Our work demonstrates that graphs derived from three out of four popular pediatric motor scales can successfully guide humanoid robots to develop these skills. The fourth scale misses some intermediate milestones that the other scales have, which causes some failures. After adding a missing milestone in its graph, it also enables the robot to develop those skills successfully.

papers.title: Sharp Holder regularity for autonomous Beltrami equations
papers.abstract: Let $Ω\subset\mathbb C$ be a domain and let $\mathcal H:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be Lipschitz with constant $0<k<1$. We prove that every weak $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ solution of the autonomous Beltrami equation $f_{\bar z}=\mathcal H(f_z)$ belongs to $C^{1,γ}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, where $γ=3/(2K+1)$ and $K=(1+k)/(1-k)$. The exponent is optimal, resolving the conjecture of Astala, Clop, Faraco, Jääskeläinen and Koski.

papers.title: Distributed Phase Tags: A Locality-Preserving Realification Compiler for Misty-State Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: Complex amplitudes can be simulated over real Hilbert spaces by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom. In a multipartite program, however, one globally shared phase tag is not a locality-preserving program transformation: every party would have to act on the same auxiliary system. We recast the distributed real simulation of multipartite quantum mechanics as a syntax-directed compiler into a real misty-state intermediate language. For $n$ parties we give explicit phase-reference codewords $|0\rangle_{P_n}$ and $|1\rangle_{P_n}$ on $n$ local tags and prove that the same real operator $J=XZ$ on any single tag realizes the logical action of multiplication by $i$. If a complex party-local gate is $A=A_R+iA_I$, its real translation is \[ \widehat A_j=A_R\otimes I+A_I\otimes J_j, \] which acts only on party $j$'s data and local phase tag. We prove an intertwining theorem for arbitrary finite party-local pure-state circuits, exact preservation of computational-basis measurement probabilities, preservation of the run-time interaction graph, and one-rebit-per-party overhead. For the canonical three-party GHZ program, the translation lies entirely inside the ordinary black-and-white misty gate fragment: controlled-$J$ replaces the complex phase operation, while the invariant $J_jJ_k|0\rangle_P=-|0\rangle_P$ transfers the required branch sign. This yields a short correctness proof for all four promised GHZ inputs and explains the earlier 64-path cancellation calculation at a single logical phase-code boundary. We distinguish this program realification problem from the weaker task of finding any real strategy with the same correlations, and state precisely which parts are known real-Hilbert-space simulation and which parts belong to the misty-language compilation layer developed here.

papers.title: Predictive Bandit Curriculum Reinforcement Learning via Gradient-Based Sample Group Discovery
papers.abstract: Curriculum learning, which organizes training samples according to their learning priority, has been widely adopted in reinforcement learning to improve training efficiency. However, existing methods commonly construct curriculum units using predefined data properties and estimate their utility by simply aggregating a single proxy signal from recent training history.Such designs may group samples with different optimization effects and fail to anticipate how their utility evolves in relation to the policy. We propose Predictive Gradient-based Bandit (PGB) Curriculum, which first discovers optimization-aware learning units by clustering projected sample-level gradients. PGB then employs a lightweight temporal predictor to forecast the future utility of each unit and converts the predictions into a Boltzmann sampling distribution for adaptive data allocation. Experiments across multiple model scales and reasoning benchmarks show that PGB consistently outperforms standard GRPO, difficulty-based curricula, and history-based scheduling strategies, demonstrating improved data utilization and training efficiency.

papers.title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.

papers.title: Zeeman Quantum Geometry of the Layer Pseudo-spin
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional layers coupled by position-dependent interlayer tunnelling host a layer pseudo-spin whose polarization is a controllable internal degree of freedom. We introduce the quantum geometry of this layer pseudo-spin: a mixed tensor formed from the interband Berry connection and the layer matrix element, which governs the response to an oscillating in-plane electric field. Because the layer pseudo-spin is an Ising-type scalar invariant under threefold rotation, its selection rules differ from those of a pseudovector spin. In a minimal two-band model, the layer-pseudo-spin quantum metric and Zeeman--Berry curvature are nonzero, while their zone integrals vanish. An in-plane drive therefore leaves the spatially averaged polarization unchanged at linear order but imprints a moiré-periodic intracell pattern, directly imageable by layer-resolved tunnelling. For twisted MoTe$_2$ bilayer, we quantify the local dipole modulation and identify the rectified, helicity-odd, and third-harmonic channels through which a net response appears at higher order.

papers.title: Rational Points on Drinfeld Modular Curves of Prime Level
papers.abstract: Let $q \ge 3$ be a prime power and let $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathbf{F}_q[T]$ be a nonzero prime ideal of degree $d$. We prove that $Y_0(\mathfrak{p})(\mathbf{F}_q(T))=\emptyset$ if $d \ge 4$ is even or $d>q$, and that $Y_1(\mathfrak{p})(\mathbf{F}_q(T)) = \emptyset $ for every $d \ge 3$.

papers.title: Whose Credential Is It? How Owner Attribution in Agent MemoryShapes Cross-User Account Misuse
papers.abstract: Shared long-term memory lets an LLM agent serving one user inadvertently retrieve another user's credentials, but it is unclear when such exposure leads to actual harm. We introduce a three-stage audit that separates three events: a foreign credential reaches the prompt (exposure), the agent acts with it (behavior), and the other user's account changes (state). In AppWorld, a store that mixes 763 past logins from all users retrieves another user's credential for 84.7 percent of required apps, yet agents rarely act on it. Misuse appears in a stress test where memory lacks the user's own credential and presents a single foreign one as the user's record: seven agents then use it in 80 to 94 percent of runs and change the victim's account in up to 43 percent, sometimes passing the official check. Naming the owner before or inside each credential line prevents most of this: with all else fixed, misuse falls from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs, also with name-free usernames, though owner-bound notes cost 3 to 5 successful tasks per model on clean memory. A wrongly written owner largely restores misuse; trailing owner tags and added safety instructions help only some models. Agent memory should consistently record whose credential it stores, and evaluations should measure behavior, not only exposure.

papers.title: On the Optimal Power Allocation and Performance Analysis for the HSIC-PA Aided Hybrid NOMA
papers.abstract: Hybrid non-orthogonal multiple access (H-NOMA), which leverages the complementary advantages of orthogonal multiple access (OMA) and NOMA, has emerged as a promising technique for next-generation wireless networks. This paper investigates power allocation optimization for the OMA and NOMA time slots allocated to the opportunistic user in H-NOMA systems, aiming to overcome the limitations of conventional equal power allocation strategies. Specifically, we consider an H-NOMA scheme that integrates hybrid successive interference cancellation (HSIC) with power adaptation (PA), referred to as the HSIC-PA aided H-NOMA scheme. To better adapt to practical communication scenarios, distinct power coefficients are assigned to the OMA and NOMA time slots of the opportunistic user to maximize the achievable data rate. Closed-form expressions for the optimal power allocation coefficients are derived, and simulation results validate the accuracy and effectiveness of the theoretical analysis.

papers.title: Causal Humility: Governing the Authority of Fairness Claims Under Causal Uncertainty
papers.abstract: AI systems increasingly shape consequential decisions in employment, lending, healthcare, and public services, making fairness an important problem for auditing and governance. Fairness assessment often requires more than identifying disparities in outcomes; it also requires understanding how those disparities arise. Causal approaches to algorithmic fairness address this explanatory problem by representing pathways through which protected attributes and other factors may influence outcomes. Yet causal reasoning in sociotechnical systems remains uncertain: relevant confounders may be unobserved, causal directions contested, and conclusions sensitive to modeling assumptions and representational choices. We introduce causal humility as a governance framework for managing the relationship between epistemic uncertainty and causal authority. Drawing on causal fairness research, epistemology, political philosophy, and science and technology studies, causal humility has four requirements: making consequential assumptions and omissions visible; preserving contestability across defensible causal accounts; recognizing indeterminacy as a legitimate analytical outcome; and maintaining proportionality between evidentiary support and institutional authority or action. We operationalize these requirements through Causal Cards, a documentation artifact for recording the causal basis, assumptions, omissions, model dependence, and governance implications of fairness claims. Using the UCI Adult dataset as a worked epistemic demonstration, we show how different causal discovery procedures applied to the same observational data render fairness-relevant pathways visible, absent, or unresolved. Causal humility treats such disagreement as information about the limits of what can responsibly be claimed and the authority those claims should carry.

papers.title: Evidence Sufficiency and Model Comparisons in MexRegQA: An Item-Level Audit of Mexican-Spanish Regulatory QA
papers.abstract: Similarity-gated coverage does not establish that retrieved evidence contains the facts needed to answer a question. We audit Mexican-Spanish financial-regulatory QA and find that 35 of 135 covered items lack some or all load-bearing facts. On the post-hoc full-evidence slice (n=98), eleven prompt-matched models score 95-98/98 and none differs significantly from the anchor; this does not establish equivalence. Removing evidence-defective items changes the nominal significance status of 14 of 55 pairwise comparisons. On 56 zero-evidence items, accuracy spans 33.9%-89.3%. Removing evidence from the audited items under an abstention-permitting prompt reduces accuracy by 63-81 percentage points in all ten tested legs, with no recovered items. Building on sufficient-context research, we contribute MexRegQA v1.0: 192 items with provenance and evidence-status labels, frozen retrieval evidence for 191 evaluated items, predictions, judge outputs and offline checks. The audit was outcome-aware, the later model/panel sweep reused the same questions, and all reported scores and labels rely on machine evaluation without independent human validation. We propose releasing evidence-status labels alongside grounded QA benchmarks so that model comparisons can be examined separately from evidence availability.

papers.title: SWAP: Test-Time Steerable Humanoid Whole-Body Collision Avoidance
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in human-centric environments must coordinate the entire body to traverse tight, cluttered spaces while maintaining balance. Existing methods often struggle to jointly consider dynamic stability and collision avoidance from high-dimensional perceptual inputs. Moreover, for humanoids, safe behavior is inherently multimodal: the same obstacle may admit multiple valid traversals, which is difficult to represent with a single deterministic policy. To address these challenges, we propose SWAP (Steerable Whole-body Avoidance Policy), a hierarchical framework that separates collision-aware decision making from stabilization. A high-level, perception-conditioned diffusion policy generates multimodal, collision-aware motion proposals, while a low-level whole-body RL controller tracks these proposals and maintains dynamic balance. To efficiently train the high-level policy, we obtain scalable supervision via hindsight labeling: we roll out the low-level policy under randomized commands, place obstacles only in the space that each executed motion did not sweep, so the motion is collision-free by construction, and re-render the perception the robot would have seen. At deployment, Monte Carlo sampling with simple cost signals steers the diffusion model toward safe, task-aligned behaviors without heavy reward tuning. Experiments in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid show reliable avoidance with static and dynamic obstacles. Test-time steering further enables customization, improving targeted rewards (e.g., speed, orientation, or posture) by 34% on average while maintaining a high collision avoidance rate. Together, these results support a practical solution to humanoid whole-body collision avoidance with test-time steerability. Project website: https://iscoyizj.github.io/SWAP-steerable-humanoid-oa-website/

papers.title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. Compatible projections reuse these bases, while a globally shared full core preserves the flexibility of each projection. Each client further maintains a lightweight private residual operator, whose directions are learned globally and whose coefficients remain local. Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones show substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter upload volume, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.

papers.title: An elementary proof of a tight $Δ+1$ bound for the additive chromatic number
papers.abstract: An additive coloring assigns positive integer labels to the vertices of a graph so that adjacent vertices have different sums of their neighbors' labels. The additive chromatic number $η(G)$ is the least $k$ for which labels from $[k]$ suffice. We give an elementary orientation argument proving that every finite simple graph $G$ satisfies $η(G) \leq Δ(G) + 1$. This argument yields a $(Δ(G) + 1)$-additive-coloring in polynomial time and improves upon the current best bound of $η(G) \leq Δ(G)^{2} - Δ(G) + 1$, valid for $Δ(G) \geq 2$, from Akbari, Ghanbari, Manaviyat, and Zare.

papers.title: Categorical classification of non-Fermi liquids in 2+1 dimensions
papers.abstract: A defining feature of non-Fermi liquids is a lack of the quasiparticle peak on the Fermi surface in the spectral function, which is usually realized by coupling a finite density of fermions with critical collective fluctuations. However, these features of the two- and three-point vertex functions are qualitatively the same across many non-Fermi liquids, which has made it difficult to classify them beyond the definition by negation. We point out that the four-point function in the pairing channel contains rich information that positively differentiates distinct types of non-Fermi liquids. Using the generalized notion of fixed points that captures scale-dependent universal pairing interaction, we provide a non-perturbative classification of 2+1-dimensional non-Fermi liquids. In the large Fermi momentum limit with fixed dimensionless couplings, metals coupled with long-wavelength critical fluctuations are classified into seven superuniversality classes. Each of them exhibits a unique phase diagram in the space of temperature and bare four-fermion coupling. The present work generalizes the earlier perturbative classification to strongly interacting non-Fermi liquids by leveraging kinematic constraints.

papers.title: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks
papers.abstract: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Extending an earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submissions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.

papers.title: Big Ramsey degrees and structures in relational languages
papers.abstract: We establish a precompact transfer theorem for big Ramsey structures and a uniform envelope theorem for valuation hypergraphs. These yield big Ramsey structures for generic injective relational structures in languages with finitely many symbols of each positive arity, answering the existence part of Problem~6.3.2 of Balko et al.\ [M.~Balko et al., J.~Eur.~Math.~Soc.\ 28, 2101--2150 (2026)], and refute Conjecture~4.7 of Braunfeld et al.\ [S.~Braunfeld et al., Adv.~Comb., Paper No.~4 (2024)]. We also construct a finitely constrained free amalgamation class in a finite language of maximum arity three whose Fraïssé limit has infinite singleton big Ramsey degree, giving a negative answer to the existence question in Problem~6.3.3 of Balko et al.

papers.title: LEVI: Benchmarking Visual Identity Fidelity with Verifiable Low-Entropy Constructs
papers.abstract: Modern generative models can produce visually plausible images while violating exact identity constraints. Evaluating such failures requires distinguishing violations of the requested identity from permissible variation in appearance. We introduce Low-Entropy Visual Identity (LEVI), which characterizes visual identities determined by compact facts and explicit rules. The low-entropy requirement concerns identity uncertainty, while appearance may remain diverse. We formulate identity fidelity in terms of the probability that a conditional image distribution assigns to the identities permitted by the prompt. Visual Identity Spaces (VIS) formalize this distinction by specifying admissible identity values and which different realizations express the same identity. Building on this formulation, we develop Verifiable Visual Grammar (VVG), a declarative language whose typed primitives and compositional constraints describe identity-bearing structures. Using this grammar, we build a benchmark for image generation. It assesses each output against the task's identity requirements, drawing evidence from the final pixels. The curated benchmark contains 1,375 tasks spanning 120 base identity spaces across six domains. Among ten evaluated model configurations, the highest whole-task pass rate is 58.69%. These results reveal a persistent gap between visually plausible images and faithful realization of their specified identities. Project page: https://maxiao0234.github.io/LEVI/.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Units, Flat Decisions: Hierarchical Micro-Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.abstract: Micro-expert pruning reduces the capacity of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models by removing coupled channels within routed experts. However, finer pruning granularity alone does not guarantee the preservation of downstream capabilities, as similar language-modeling perplexity can accompany substantially different task performance. We revisit micro-expert mask construction as two distinct decisions: allocating retained capacity across experts and selecting channels within that capacity. We propose UC-RAMP, a two-stage post-training pruning framework that explicitly separates these decisions. CAPE uses cross-domain calibration evidence to redistribute expert widths under an exact layer-wise budget, while RAMP refines channel composition at fixed widths through one-out, one-in exchanges guided by a channel-interaction surrogate. Across three MoE models at 25% and 50% routed-expert channel pruning, UC-RAMP achieves the highest ten-task mean accuracy among evaluated pruning methods in five of six settings. At 50% pruning, it outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 8.19, 3.96, and 6.14 percentage points across the three models, respectively. In a single-A100 deployment at 25% pruning, UC-RAMP reduces measured time to first token by 19.7--23.9% and time per output token by 20.2--22.3% relative to the unpruned model. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/UC_RAMP.

papers.title: Velocity-resolved Ionization Mapping of the Broad-line Region. II. Signatures of Eccentric Broad-line Regions from a Quantitative Photoionization-Based Model
papers.abstract: Velocity-resolved reverberation mapping (RM) is one of the most powerful tools for probing the geometry and kinematics of the broad-line region in active galactic nuclei. However, its interpretation may be non-unique, as similar velocity-delay signatures can arise from different combinations of BLR geometry and kinematics. To address this degeneracy, this series of studies develops velocity-resolved ionization mapping (IM) as a complementary technique. In this second paper of the series, we construct photoionization-based BLR models to quantitatively demonstrate the diagnostic power of the joint RM+IM framework. We calculate local \ha\ and \hb\ emissivities with Cloudy, couple them with disk-like BLR models, and generate synthetic velocity-dependent line fluxes, lags, and Balmer decrements. The model reproduces the observed anti-correlation between the integrated BD and the incident ionizing continuum, with scatter naturally introduced by reverberation delays. We show that a virialized elliptical BLR can produce diverse velocity-delay maps and velocity-resolved lags that mimic RM signatures commonly attributed to virialized motion, inflow, or outflow. In contrast, the velocity-resolved BD is sensitive to the symmetry of the BLR gas distribution, providing a key diagnostic for distinguishing eccentric geometry from non-virial motions. Through proof-of-concept comparisons with one double-peaked and one single-peaked AGN, we show that an elliptical-disk BLR can simultaneously reproduce the observed line profiles, velocity-resolved lags, and velocity-resolved BDs. These results provide a quantitative basis for IM, support the presence of eccentric BLR structures in AGNs, and demonstrate the potential of joint RM+IM analyses to break the BLR geometry-kinematics degeneracy.

papers.title: The Eighth-Order Evolution Model for Closed Planar Curves
papers.abstract: We consider the $L^2(ds)$ gradient flow of $\frac12\int k_{ss}^2\,ds$ for smooth closed immersed planar curves. The stationary curves are precisely the multiply covered circles. We give an explicit sufficient condition under which the elastic energy is non-increasing and for each nonzero turning number, explicit small initial scale-invariant energy yields a global smooth solution with bounded positive length and exponential convergence to a fixed multiply covered circle, after reparametrisation. We note that that the qualitative rigidity and convergence results are already contained in the generalised ideal flow theory of McCoy and Wheeler. The present paper gives quantitative measure of small initial data, corrected evolution identities, and a complete argument in the case of the curvature energy $\frac12\int k_{ss}^2\,ds$.

papers.title: Uniqueness of twisted linear periods
papers.abstract: Let $F$ be a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic zero, and let $\D$ be either $F$ or a quaternion division algebra over $F$. We prove that every irreducible smooth representation of $\GL_{p+q}(\D)$ has at most one linear period transforming under any prescribed character of $\GL_p(\D)\times\GL_q(\D)$.

papers.title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
papers.abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

papers.title: Enhancing Lunar PNT Performance Through Surface Station Enabled Radiometric Observables
papers.abstract: Future lunar surface missions require reliable positioning for autonomous rover operations. Lunar navigation satellite systems may provide limited vertical positioning accuracy due to satellite availability and observation geometry, particularly during early deployment. This study investigates a radiometric navigation architecture in which a lunar surface station (SS) improves rover positioning through double-differenced satellite observations and additional surface-to-surface ranging. Pseudorange and Doppler measurements from lunar navigation satellites are used for relative positioning between the SS and rover, while dual one-way ranging (DOWR) provides an additional range observable. The radiometric solution is integrated with rover dead-reckoning information. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using five satellites representative of NASA's Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) constellation and a rover trajectory near Connecting Ridge at the lunar south pole. The results show that the SS improves horizontal and vertical relative positioning, with further gains from DOWR. In the simulated scenario, the mean 99.7% vertical positioning error decreased from 29.9 m without the SS to 5.5 m with double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler processing, and to 4.8 m with DOWR. An uncorrected DOWR hardware bias significantly degraded positioning, whereas the proposed bias-estimation method achieved a final estimation error of 0.058 +/- 0.057 m. The benefit of DOWR also depended on observation geometry. These results demonstrate the potential of a lunar surface station to improve vertical relative positioning through direct radiometric ranging, complementing its communication and navigation support roles.

papers.title: Corrected Block Sparse Spectral Optimization: Exact Models, Finite Identification, and Local Dynamics
papers.abstract: The block generalized-power method pairs threshold-based support selection with inexpensive Stiefel updates, but the standard block formulation conflates two nonequivalent objectives and leaves inactive components, threshold ties, and post-selection refitting ill-specified. We rebuild the model from the primal. Eliminating each loading column from the normalized loading-ball problem gives a sum of soft-thresholded Euclidean norms (A-SUM); the squared-threshold objective in common use arises from a quadratic lift (A-SQ). We prove both identities, exhibit a two-component instance whose maximizers disagree, and specify explicit conventions for zero-response columns, ties, rank deficiency, and mask-before-refit. For A-SQ we separate the historical full-polar iteration from a safeguarded Riemannian ascent and prove, for the latter, whole-sequence convergence via a sufficient-ascent lemma, a relative-error lemma, and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, which applies because the soft-threshold objective and the Stiefel constraint are semi-algebraic. A strict threshold margin then forces finite identification of the support and sign pattern. The post-identification map is ordinary power iteration on the active covariance for a rank-one hard threshold, and the Frechet derivative of a coupled polar map for component-specific supports; a radius-based safe-screening rule follows from the same local analysis. Planted-spike experiments match the predicted identification time and local rates. On modern-AI panels (GPT-2 residual stream, ViT CLS stream, Pitprops) the thresholded block-sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and improve on it in monosemanticity and class specialisation. On three native-label scRNA datasets (Zheng17 FACS-sorted PBMCs, 68k donor-A with FACS-correlated labels, Tabula Muris) A-SQ beats dense PCA on cluster-recovery AMI by +0.023 to +0.044 at matched sparsity.

papers.title: Frobenius Profiles of Polynomial-Multiple MRD Codes
papers.abstract: We study Frobenius intersection profiles of maximum rank distance (MRD) codes arising from ordinary polynomial multiples over finite fields. We prove that every numerically admissible profile is realized within this family over every sufficiently large extension, using a root-exponent pattern independent of the extension degree. A factor-orbit gap formula provides the underlying structural description, while effective extension-degree bounds guarantee realization. We also establish a lower bound valid for all polynomial generators and show that the upper and lower bounds differ by only $O_q(\log n)$ along an infinite family of parameters. Finally, we characterize the generalized Gabidulin members and obtain non-generalized-Gabidulin realizations of every profile with initial loss at least two over infinitely many extensions.

papers.title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer's coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

papers.title: Inside the Scorer: Mechanistic Evidence on Rubric Control in LLM-Based Automated Essay Scoring from 25 Base Models
papers.abstract: Automated essay scoring (AES) using large language models (LLMs) offers promising use cases for language assessment, yet high-stakes testing requires scores that are both controllable and verifiable, which current LLM-based scorers lack. Given that, we investigate whether LLM-based scorers form distinct internal representations for individual scoring rubrics and whether these representations can be independently controlled. Probing and steering 25 open-weight base LLMs (0.13B-10.31B parameters; 14 families) on human-scored BESTEP English writing tasks, we find that holistic scores are decodable from model activations for the longer tasks (Parts 2 and 3) and only weakly for the shortest (Part 1). Furthermore, scoring rubrics have partly separable directions in representation space for the longer tasks, though not for short responses (Part 1). However, causal steering reveals a critical limitation: applying a matching intervention (e.g., steering "grammar" on a grammar-degraded response) yields only a negligible advantage (about 2% of the effect) over a mismatched intervention (e.g., steering "vocabulary"), and none that is detectable in any of the 10 testable comparisons across reliably measured rubrics. Rather than controlling distinct evaluative dimensions, the rubric directions share a dominant lever whose rubric-specific parts are not selective, which may mirror the halo structure of human ratings. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we show that analytic scoring rubrics designed for human raters do not behave as independent controls in base LLMs, even among the seven models whose scores agree best with human raters ($r \geq 0.6$). Second, we establish a methodology that shows that score agreement and decodability do not imply rubric-level control in LLM-based assessment.

papers.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.

papers.title: Iterative Truncated SVD for Inverse Scattering Problems
papers.abstract: We propose an iterative truncated SVD (iTSVD) algorithm based on a nonlinear least squares formulation for Newton's method for inverse scattering problems. The key idea is to estimate the effective rank of the corresponding linearized operator (or the Jacobian matrix after discretization), which defines the dimension of the signal space of the associated forward operator. Once the effective rank is estimated, truncated SVD (TSVD) reconstruction in the signal space can be computed efficiently based on fast random SVD (RSVD) -- only requiring matrix-vector multiplication which can be implemented in a matrix-free formulation by solving multiple forward and adjoint problems of the same type. Our analysis and numerical experiments show that iTSVD can markedly improve computational efficiency by reducing the number of iterations and enhance stability by physics/information based inversion. Moreover, the effective rank estimate is naturally model- and data-based. Extensive experiments, including far- or near-field, limited aperture, and random measurement data without or with noise, are presented.

papers.title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems
papers.abstract: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.

papers.title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.

papers.title: Neural Video Coding under Limited Delay: Theoretical Optimality and System Design
papers.abstract: Traditional neural video compression (NVC) methods predominantly follow strictly causal predictive-coding paradigm, treating zero-frame delay as a fixed constraint rather than delay as an explicit design parameter. From an information-theoretic perspective, allowing limited frame delay enables a codec to exploit correlations with future frames within the delay window, thereby reducing uncertainty that is inaccessible to strictly causal prediction and potentially improving the rate-distortion tradeoff. In this work, we formalize this intuition through a rigorous rate-distortion analysis builds on the clique factorization of Markov networks, and propose Graph-Factored Sequential Coding (GFSC), a principled framework for sequential video coding under limited delay. To our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical result showing that, for general $K$-order Markov sources with positive distributions, a $K$-frame delay is sufficient to attain joint-coding rate-distortion optimality over a nontrivial distortion region, a guarantee unavailable to zero-delay causal coding in general. In practice, we instantiate GFSC through lightweight neural modules, allowing existing causal predictive codecs to be augmented without modifying their core architectures. Experiments across multiple NVC models and datasets show that GFSC consistently improves rate-distortion performance over the corresponding causal counterparts. Under matched delay budgets, GFSC also achieves competitive performance compared with representative bidirectional codecs.

papers.title: Estimation and Inference for the Joint Autoregressive Quantile-Expected Shortfall Model
papers.abstract: Expected shortfall is defined as the truncated mean of a random variable that falls below a specified quantile level and is widely recognized as an important risk measure. Motivated by the empirical observation of clustering patterns in financial risks, we consider a joint autoregressive model for both conditional quantile and expected shortfall. Existing estimation methods for such models typically rely on minimizing a nonlinear and nonconvex joint loss function, which is challenging to solve. We introduce a two-step regression framework to estimate the model parameters with theoretical guarantees. We further develop a Portmanteau test for model diagnostics and prove its asymptotic validity for Type I error control. Our empirical results on stock market data indicate that the proposed models effectively capture the clustering patterns and leverage effects on the conditional expected shortfall.

papers.title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration? Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams
papers.abstract: LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.

papers.title: Characteristic cycles and non-acyclicity classes for constructible étale sheaves
papers.abstract: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism between smooth schemes over a perfect field $k$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a constructible sheaf on $X$ and $Z$ a closed subscheme of $X$ such that $f$ is $SS(\mathcal F)$-transversal outside $Z$. We construct a class supported on the non-transversal locus $Z$ by using the characteristic cycle $CC(\mathcal F)$ defined by T. Saito. This class is a geometric counterpart of the non-acyclicity class introduced by the third author and Zhao in [Invent. Math. 240 (2025), 123-191]. Under certain conditions, the formation of this class is compatible with base change and proper pushforward. It also satisfies the Milnor formula and a conductor formula. We conjecture that the image of this geometric class under the cycle class map is the non-acyclicity class. This conjecture can be viewed as a (relative version of) Milnor-type formula for non-isolated singularities. We prove this conjecture when $k$ is algebraically closed, $X$ is quasi-affine and $Y=\mathbb A^1_k$.

papers.title: TimelineAgent: An LLM-based Framework for Query-Centric Event Timeline Extraction Across Multiple Documents
papers.abstract: Query-centric cross-document event timeline extraction aims to construct event timelines from multiple documents under diverse query focuses. The task is very challenging due to the heterogeneous event modeling and reasoning requirements arising from both the intrinsic complexity of cross-document timeline construction and the diversity of query focuses. In this paper, we propose TimelineAgent, an LLM-based multi-agent framework featuring a multi-stage reasoning workflow, where heterogeneous event features are organized into reusable skills and orchestrated through a goal-oriented protocol. To facilitate evaluation, we construct a benchmark covering diverse query focuses. Experimental results show that TimelineAgent consistently outperforms existing methods, offering a practical framework for complex real-world timeline construction.

papers.title: Think Densely, Act Sparsely: Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving. We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space. In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving). The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model. Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference. This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning. These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.

papers.title: Computational assessment of incremental pyriform aperture enlargement in plastic surgery: effect on inhaled nasal airflow
papers.abstract: Background. The pyriform aperture is a critical anterior bony constriction governing nasal airflow and is clinically relevant to both functional and aesthetic nasal surgery, yet the degree of pyriform aperture enlargement (PAE) needed to capture its aerodynamic benefit is undefined. This study employs high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to quantify the aerodynamic effects of progressive PAE and identify a threshold beyond which further enlargement yields minimal benefit. Methods. A CT-derived three-dimensional nasal airway model was digitally modified to produce baseline, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% increases in pyriform aperture cross-sectional area. Pressure-driven large-eddy simulations (LES) were performed at a fixed transnasal pressure difference of 11.25 Pa to quantify changes in inspiratory flow rate, total airway resistance, and local airflow characteristics. Results. Progressive PAE monotonically increased inspiratory flow from 15.063 to 15.252 L/min (approximately 1.25%) and reduced airway resistance from 0.6138 to 0.6028 Pa.min/L (approximately 1.80%). The aerodynamic response was strongly nonlinear, with the greatest improvement occurring between 10% and 15% enlargement. Increasing the aperture from 15% to 20% produced negligible additional improvement. Conclusions. PAE improves nasal airflow by reducing the resistance imposed by the anterior bony constriction. In the anatomical model investigated, approximately 15% area enlargement represented an efficient aerodynamic threshold, after which the dominant resistance shifted toward downstream nasal structures and further enlargement produced little additional benefit. These findings support a conservative, anatomy-dependent approach to PAE and warrant validation across a broader range of patient-specific geometries.

papers.title: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
papers.abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.

papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: Collective Experience Learning Across 96 Robots
papers.abstract: Robot deployment generates experience that can support policy improvement, but continued reliance on expert corrective actions makes learning difficult to scale across growing fleets. We propose learning from fleet experience: using deployed robots' own executions as a source of supervision for further policy improvement. We call this paradigm Collective Experience Learning (CEL), in which robots pool execution experience to update a shared policy that returns to the fleet. Following expert-supervised initialization, we realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT). FERT uses failure contexts to retrieve relevant segments from successful trajectories and prioritizes their recorded actions for supervised updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. Operators provide binary episode-outcome labels and environment resets. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates robot execution, cloud inference and policy optimization despite local interruptions. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and generally improve performance across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots raises success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support CEL as a scalable approach to improving robot policy reliability through experience generated during deployment.

papers.title: Linear Group Actions with Exactly One Regular Orbit
papers.abstract: Let $p$ be an odd prime, $G$ a finite $p$-group, and $V$ a finite faithful irreducible $G$-module. We show that if $G$ has exactly one regular orbit on $V$, then $p=2^{n}-1$ is a Mersenne prime and $(G,V)$ embeds into $(P_m,V_m)$ for some $m\ge 1$, where $P_m$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of the monomial group ${\rm GL}_1(2^{n})\wr S_{p^{m-1}}$ and $V_m$ is its natural module, regarded over ${\Bbb F}_2$. We determine the largest orbit size $p^{x_m}$ of $P_m$ on $V_m$ and the number of orbits of this size, and we construct subgroups of $P_m$ of order $p^{x_m}$ whose unique regular orbit is a largest orbit of $P_m$; for $p=3$ such subgroups exist for every $m$, whereas for Mersenne primes $p\ge 7$ we prove that they exist only for $m\ge 3$. Finally, we classify the subgroups of $P_m$ of order $p^{x_m}$ with exactly one regular orbit for $m=2$ and, with the help of a computer, for $p=3$ and $m=3$, where there are $13$ such pairs up to isomorphism; for $p=3$ and $m=4$ we show that there are exactly $4914$ conjugacy classes of such subgroups in $P_4$. In particular, such a subgroup is in general not determined by its regular orbit.

papers.title: Reduced Molecular Plasma Kinetics with Non-Boltzmann Vibrational Distribution
papers.abstract: Vibrational kinetics can strongly affect energy transfer, chemical kinetics, and discharge behavior in molecular plasmas, but resolving all internal states is often impractical for reactor-scale simulation. Compact, physics-based vibrational closures are particularly needed when complete state-to-state (StS) data are limited. Starting from a detailed $\mathrm{H}_2$ StS plasma-kinetics framework coupled to an electron-Boltzmann calculation, this work develops a reduced vibrational-kinetics formulation. The $\mathrm{H}_2$ vibrational ladder is reduced to two non-Boltzmann groups that evolve their population and internal energy. State-resolved reaction rates and associated energy-exchange terms are projected onto the groups for subsequent tabulation in reactor-scale plasma models. StS-informed samples of the reduced-model are propagated for pulsed RF $\mathrm{H}_2$ plasmas across a scan of pulse-averaged absorbed power and compared with the corresponding StS simulations. Predictions from the sampled models reproduce the bulk plasma response, including electron density, atomic-H density, and $\mathrm{H}_3^+$ density. Discrepancies in $\mathrm{H}^-$ production and the upper-energy-group vibrational temperature persist across the sampled reductions. This indicates a limitation of the present VDF reconstruction rather than the nominal parameter choice. Tail-sensitive processes therefore require a more accurate representation of the vibrational distribution.

papers.title: How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost? Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles
papers.abstract: Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability $\varepsilon$, the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change $k$ facts is accepted with probability $1/k$, so it costs one fact on average. Rules with $s$ premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by $r$ rules can cost order $r^{1-1/s}$ facts. For entity resolution with $m$ records of one entity, the first-order risk equals $\varepsilon$ times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order $m^{1/3}$; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large $m$, worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.

papers.title: Free boundary regularity for the porous medium equation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we resolve the local cone conjecture proposed by Kienzler, Koch, and Vázquez concerning the free-boundary regularity of the porous medium equation. We prove that the local cone condition guarantees the smoothness of the free boundary lying outside the initial support. The proof relies on new gradient estimates obtained through maximum principle arguments and comparison principles. As an application, we establish the global-in-time smoothness of the free boundary for solutions with convex initial support under standard assumptions on the initial data.

papers.title: Compiling Environment Classifiers to Contextual Modal Types
papers.abstract: Type systems for metaprogramming take one of two approaches to safeguarding the scopes of variables in generated code. They either use Environment Classifiers (EC) to identify scopes by name (Taha and Nielsen, 2003), or they use Contextual Modal Type Theory (CMTT) to match scopes by structure (Nanevski, Pfenning, and Pientka, 2008). In this paper, we connect these two approaches by compiling a calculus with polymorphic environment classifiers, subtyping, and mutable references to a CMTT-based calculus with polymorphic contexts, mutable references, and first-class substitutions. The key idea is to map each environment classifier to a context. We prove that the compilation preserves types and that compilation preserves the behavior of metaprograms. Both proofs are mechanized in Agda. The compilation shows that CMTT is at least as expressive as environment classifiers. We conjecture that the converse compilation is difficult, because environment classifiers impose a stricter regime on the metaprogram.

papers.title: Functional Cross-layer Experts Routing for One-step Diffusion Distillation
papers.abstract: One-step distillation compresses diffusion trajectories into a single forward evaluation, yet how internal capacity should be structured within that remaining pass remains largely unexplored. In this setting, identical parameters must simultaneously preserve general generative priors and resolve prompt-specific details without iterative refinement. We formalize this challenge as functional allocation. Our analysis reveals that decoupling representations is beneficial only when expert interference outweighs shared transfer, favoring an always-active shared backbone augmented with conditionally routed residuals over standard isolated MoE architectures. We propose DeMoE, which pairs a persistent shared expert with conditionally routed expert slices across image FFNs, trained under a one-step distribution-matching objective with executed-route supervision. On one-step FLUX.2-4B generation, DeMoE achieves a GenEval score of 0.8220 while activating only 80.5% of the image-FFN width, substantially outperforming dense one-step baselines, matching the 50-step teacher overall, and surpassing it on complex composition and counting. Across COCO-10K, DeMoE establishes state-of-the-art fidelity and diversity among single-step models, demonstrating that structured internal computation reallocation provides a superior compression paradigm for diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/toffeecat/demoe-ttt-router.

papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the optimal masked-gradient communication rate for every feasible dropout scenario and the optimal mask-elimination communication rate in almost all feasible regimes. Its key rate and key-distribution communication rate are each optimal or within a factor of two of their respective information-theoretic optima. These results characterize the fundamental randomness and communication costs of secure aggregation with user dropouts.

papers.title: AdaptAD: Foundation Model Adaptation with Missing Modality Robustness for Alzheimer's Disease Staging Across the Disease Continuum
papers.abstract: Staging Alzheimer's disease (AD) across its continuum, from cognitively normal (CN) through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia from a single structural MRI remains difficult because 3-D networks overfit small cohorts, and FreeSurfer morphometry is often unavailable. We present AdaptAD, which reads a registered T1-weighted scan as 16 anatomically placed 2.5-D slices through the medial temporal lobe and adapts a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), training 3.5 M of 89 M parameters. Morphometry enters as tokens when present, or as a learned [MISSING] token, and a missing-aware stacker fuses both experts. Under a pre-registered protocol, ten methods were compared for three-class CN/MCI/AD staging on identical 5-fold splits of 597 ADNI participants, 29% without FreeSurfer, with Holm-corrected paired bootstrap tests. The locked model was tested once on 993 OASIS-3 participants (988 scored by every method). On ADNI, AdaptAD achieved a three-class macro-AUC of 0.745 (95% CI 0.709 to 0.781), ranking first and significantly exceeding full fine-tuning, ShaSpec and a 3-D CNN. On OASIS-3 it reached 0.780 (0.748 to 0.814), and on the CDR-based label (0.804) it significantly outperformed every 3-D and image-tabular method. LoRA matched full fine-tuning with 25 times fewer trainable parameters, and removing morphometry changed external macro-AUC by less than 0.003. The disease score tracked MMSE and CDR-SB within diagnostic groups and stratified MCI-to-dementia progression (log-rank p < 0.001), while saliency concentrated in medial temporal and periventricular regions. A parameter-efficient 2-D foundation model can therefore stage the full AD continuum from a routine T1 scan without morphometry, offering a scalable route to memory-clinic deployment.

papers.title: Using Bayesian Sequential Logistic Regression to Model the Organ Transplant Selection Process
papers.abstract: Organ transplantation evaluation is a multi-stage process in which only patients who complete one stage remain eligible for the next, leading to patient attrition and reducing later-stage sample sizes. Covariate associations may differ across decision points, and identifying these stage-specific effects is necessary to target interventions and understand disparities. Conventional approaches that model each transition independently fail to distinguish stage-specific from shared associations and tend to produce imprecise estimates at later stages. We propose a Bayesian sequential logistic regression (BSLR) framework that represents progression as conditional Bernoulli distributions within a joint likelihood that preserves chronological ordering; we further show its equivalence to an adjusted continuation-ratio model. A hierarchical prior decomposes each covariate effect into an overall effect and a transition-specific deviation. This partial-pooling structure shares information across stages and stabilizes estimation where data are sparse, while a masking mechanism accommodates covariates structurally unavailable at particular stages without discarding records or imputing values. In simulations, BSLR achieved lower bias, posterior variance, and mean squared error than independent logistic regression. We demonstrated the utility of our model using a cohort of patients referred for kidney or liver transplant. Posterior estimates indicated that the associations of clinical indicators and social determinants of health with progression differed across care continuum phases. BSLR identified stage-specific heterogeneity in covariate associations, revealing factors whose effects reversed direction across evaluation stages and detecting associations at late-stage transitions that independent models failed to resolve due to insufficient precision.

papers.title: Combinatorial Calabi flows on infinitely triangulated surfaces
papers.abstract: We study the combinatorial Calabi flow associated with vertex scalings on infinitely triangulated surfaces with piecewise Euclidean and piecewise hyperbolic metrics. Under the assumptions of uniformly bounded vertex degree and an $ε$-uniformly nondegenerate initial metric, we establish short-time existence of smooth solutions and prove uniqueness among solutions that are continuous in the $L^\infty$ norm.

papers.title: Berry--Esseen Bounds for High-Temperature Ising Models
papers.abstract: We consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and establish sharp results for the normal approximation of the magnetisation throughout the high-temperature regime. In particular, we establish optimal Berry--Esseen bounds between the magnetisation in an arbitrary finite region and a Gaussian with the corresponding finite-volume variance. These results hold for finite-volume Gibbs measures with arbitrary boundary conditions, as well as for the infinite-volume Gibbs measure. We also determine sharp rates of convergence of the magnetisation in a finite box to a Gaussian with variance given by the infinite-volume susceptibility. For this fixed Gaussian target, we show that, in dimensions $d\ge 3$, periodic boundary conditions yield strictly faster convergence than free boundary conditions. Our approach uses Stein's method to quantify the normal approximation error by analysing the semigroup of the continuous-time Ising heat-bath dynamics.

papers.title: Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models: Closing the Loop between Hypotheses and Experiments
papers.abstract: Scientific model discovery requires proposing candidate models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. However, LLM-based approaches typically rely on in-context learning to predict outcomes and select experiments, lacking explicit model evaluation to systematically guide hypothesis search, while Bayesian approaches enable principled model comparison but are confined to a predefined candidate set which results in limited search spaces. To this end, we introduce BMD, which closes the loop between LLM-driven hypothesis generation and Bayesian experimental design. Specifically, an LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits their parameters, weighs them by model evidence, and averages their predictions. Then, BMD chooses the next experimental conditions by maximizing the joint expected information gain over families and their parameters, while feeding the updated beliefs and residual diagnostics back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, BMD achieves lowest final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents while recovering exact functional forms more often, with ablations supporting numerical feedback and the joint objective.

papers.title: MAPS: A Multi-Agent Personalized Script-Driven Video Advertising System Enhanced by Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: With the rapid growth of online video consumption, video advertising has become a dominant component of digital advertising. Most personalized video advertising systems follow a retrieval-based paradigm, which matches ad content with user preferences in a feature space and recommends the most similar candidates. However, since the candidate creatives are pre-produced, this paradigm limits the granularity of personalization and leads to performance disparities across diverse user groups. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-agent personalized script-driven video advertising system (MAPS). We design four collaborative agents that form a closed-loop pipeline of user profile modeling, script generation, video synthesis, and feedback-driven iterative refinement. To train the Scripter Agent, we develop a reinforcement learning framework equipped with a multi-dimensional reward function, which steers the agent toward producing scripts that simultaneously align with user content preferences and target product information. Extensive offline experiments on representative datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves encouraging performance in generating and integrating personalized creatives. Online A/B experiments in a specific scenario in the Kuaishou advertising system show that MAPS improves CTR by 2.87%, CVR by 2.74%, and ARPU by 9.85% over the generative baseline.

papers.title: Cognitively Decoupled Meta-Induction for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) tackles downstream tasks conditioned on demonstrations. This paradigm relies heavily on neighbor-based matching between queries and demonstrations, limiting out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. For better generalization, rule-based inductive reasoning derives task-level regularities, which we term task-level inductive representations (TIR), before directly answering. However, existing methods lack generalizable inductive ability across diverse tasks. Inspired by meta-learning, we propose Cognitive-Decoupling meta-Induction (CoDI) for TIR-based inductive reasoning on general tasks. CoDI comprises a Cognitive-Decoupling Framework for query-blind TIR induction, and a Dual-Loop Meta-Inductive Learning method for cross-task inducer optimization. Empirically, CoDI achieves substantial performance gains on five ID and OOD benchmarks, and preserves OOD gains without explicit induction at inference. Code is available at https://github.com/Yuqian-Wang2277/codi-meta-induction.

papers.title: On the Hausdorff dimension of oscillatory motions in three-body problems
papers.abstract: We show that for the Sitnikov example and for the restricted planar circular 3-body problem the set of oscillatory motions often has maximal Hausdorff dimension. Also, we construct Newhouse domains for both problems.

papers.title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.

papers.title: Which Answers Agree? Evaluating Self-Consistency from Incomplete Logs
papers.abstract: Self-consistency answers a question by generating multiple responses and selecting the most frequent answer. Its evaluation requires both correctness labels and information about which responses agree; correctness labels alone generally determine neither voting accuracy nor the benefit of additional votes. For tasks in which all correct responses map to the same normalized answer, we derive sharp accuracy bounds using classical stochastic majorization, refined by abstention counts and answer-category limits. We also derive sharp bounds on accuracy changes across voting budgets that share a response pool. When answer-category counts are available, we introduce Plurality-U, a count-based dynamic program that exactly averages voting accuracy over all fixed-size subsets, eliminating finite-pool Monte Carlo error. On 1,403,520 stored outputs from recent reasoning models in Scorio Lite and Scorio Trace, recording abstention counts and answer options cuts the width of SuperGPQA accuracy intervals by more than half. For moving from 9 to 17 votes, our bounds reduce interval width by a median of 77.7% on SuperGPQA and 72.3% on 14 GPQA and Adaptive-Consistency pools, compared with a baseline that combines separate accuracy bounds.
