We establish consistency of an \(m\)-out-of-\(n\) parametric bootstrap when \(m\to\infty\) and \(m/n\to0\). Numerical studies assess the approximation and distinguish bootstrap and optimization errors; a flow-cytometry application illustrates uncertainty summaries invariant to component labeling under a working mixture model.

papers.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

papers.title: Effects of Nonmagnetic Impurities on Nonequilibrium Phase Transitions in Microwave-Driven Superconductors
papers.abstract: We investigate the nonequilibrium steady states of a microwave-driven BCS superconductor in the presence of nonmagnetic impurity scattering and energy relaxation. Using the Floquet-Nambu-Keldysh Green's function method together with the self-consistent Born approximation, we self-consistently determine the superconducting order parameter in the microwave-driven steady state. We find that the nonequilibrium phase diagram depends strongly on the impurity-scattering strength. When impurity scattering is absent or weak, the steady-state order parameter is single-valued at each temperature and drive frequency. At intermediate scattering strengths, we find bistability between microwave-enhanced and microwave-suppressed superconducting states. As the impurity-scattering strength increases further, we instead find bistability between the superconducting and normal states. This evolution reflects competition between two effects of microwave driving: Eliashberg-type enhancement through the redistribution of thermally excited quasiparticles and suppression through pair-breaking-induced quasiparticle generation. In contrast to the robustness of equilibrium $s$-wave superconductivity against nonmagnetic impurity scattering, our results demonstrate that nonmagnetic impurity scattering plays a central role in determining the character of nonequilibrium superconducting phase transitions under microwave driving.

papers.title: Adaptive Decoding Methods for Token-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.

papers.title: ActionRoPE: Action as Coordinates for Spatially Consistent Control in Planar-Camera Game World Models
papers.abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/.

papers.title: A Morphology-Based Cross-Tracer Ratio for Robust BAO Tests
papers.abstract: We use the Cross-Tracer Clustering Ratio (CTCR) acoustic response estimator, a new probe of morphology-dependent galaxy clustering in photometric surveys. CTCR is the ratio of the auto-power spectrum of early-type galaxies (ETGs) to their cross-power spectrum with late-type galaxies (LTGs). In the matched-kernel deterministic linear-bias limit the CTCR cancels the complete projected matter spectrum, including the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) wiggles, leaving only the relative linear bias. This makes the ratio uniquely sensitive to physics beyond deterministic linear bias: any residual acoustic structure in the CTCR must arise from a difference between the normalised non-linear responses of the two tracers. We, for the first time, exploit this property to model the measured ratio as a smooth scale-dependent baseline multiplied by a scale-dependent acoustic template, and constrain the amplitude $A_{\rm morph}$ of the differential acoustic response jointly with the BAO dilation parameter $α$. Applying the estimator to nine bins of the DESI Legacy Survey Data Release 8 spanning $0.1 < z < 0.9$, we obtain$α= 0.9997 \pm 0.0383$, consistent with the Planck 2018 $Λ$CDM prediction, and $A_{\rm morph} = 0.369 \pm 0.307$, consistent with zero. A Bayesian model comparison yields at most a 2.6$σ$ preference for the acoustic template over a smooth-only baseline. The estimator is model-independent, requires no external calibration of the absolute bias, and is directly applicable to the wide-field imaging surveys that will define the next decade of cosmology. It offers a new route to testing halo occupation and assembly-bias models, and an independent, systematics-robust cross-check of BAO measurements from spectroscopic surveys.

papers.title: k-Submodular Cover Problem with a Matroid Constraint
papers.abstract: We investigate k-submodular cover problem with a matroid constraint on an n-element ground set V , which seeks k disjoint subsets of V with minimal cost, where their union is an independent set for some matroid defined on V and the k-submodular utility function surpasses a specified threshold. This problem generalizes the k-submodular cover problem and has a wide range of applications in artificial intelligence and combinatorial optimization. In this paper, we propose a matroid extended greedy algorithm for this problem, analyze its bi-criteria approximation ratio, and further derive an improved approximation ratio under the special case of unit costs.

papers.title: On Multi-label radio Labelings of Graphs
papers.abstract: We propose and study a multi-labeling generalization of the $k$-radio labeling problem of graphs: given a graph $G$ and integers $k$ and $m$, assign to each vertex of $G$ a set of $m$ integer labels such that distinct labels assigned to a vertex differ by at least $k+1$, and the labels of any two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ pairwise differ by at least $k+1-d(x,y)$, with $d(x,y)$ being the distance between vertices $x$ and $y$. We prove general bounds on the minimum span of such a labeling and more refined results for the case $k=1$. For paths and cycles, we derive sharp bounds on the minimum span when $k$ is small. We finally propose a conjecture for the minimum span on the path and for an almost-tight bound on the cycle.

papers.title: Mixed Chern curvature on complete flags
papers.abstract: We prove that the complete flag manifold SU(m)/T m-1, with m >= 3 and its standard complex structure, admits no invariant Hermitian metric with constant mixed Chern curvature when the coefficient of the holomorphic sectional curvature is nonzero. This extends the preceding nonexistence result for a particular Wallach metric on SU(3)/T2 to all invariant Hermitian metrics and to complete type-A flags of arbitrary dimension. Curvature evaluations on holomorphic root spheres contradict a necessary trace identity, covering both Kahler and non-Kahler invariant metrics and excluding both zero and nonzero curvature constants.

papers.title: Minimum-Cost Robust Evidence Certificates for Horn Reasoning under Correlated Source Failures
papers.abstract: A small justification for a rule-based conclusion may disappear when a source is withdrawn, and multiple derivations need not provide independent evidence. We study minimum-cost certificates that preserve a Horn conclusion under every withdrawal of at most k source domains. Evidence records remain distinct from asserted facts, supporting replicated attestations and overlapping failure dependencies. Transversals of minimal-support footprints characterize robustness and explain why disjoint-proof requirements can reject valid certificates. An exact procedure alternates weighted evidence selection with a source-failure oracle. A rule-closed counterinterpretation yields a globally valid selection cut without enumerating supports or failure scenarios. We prove correctness, finite termination, and cost optimality, establish coNP-completeness of unrestricted verification and NP-completeness of synthesis for every fixed budget, and identify a tractable reachability restriction. Experiments on controlled benchmarks, reachability graphs, and ontology-derived instances demonstrate that our counterinterpretation-guided synthesis achieves up to 92% optimum coverage within practical resource bounds, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction while confirming the necessity of transversal-based reasoning over proof-packing heuristics.

papers.title: Hostbusters: constraining $H_0$ and binary formation channels through gravitational-wave host galaxy associations
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave dark sirens can be combined with galaxy catalogues to provide a measurement of the Hubble constant. This inference requires assigning each potential host galaxy a probability of hosting a merger, but the appropriate weighting is uncertain because the binary merger rate may trace different galaxy properties, such as stellar mass or star formation rate, depending on the underlying formation channel. We introduce a flexible framework in which the dark-siren population is described as a mixture of two host-weighting prescriptions, with the mixing fraction inferred jointly with $H_0$. These components may be interpreted as subpopulations associated with distinct binary-formation environments. Using simulated catalogues, we show that marginalising over uncertainty in the host-population mixture preserves unbiased constraints on $H_0$, while allowing the gravitational-wave data to constrain the relative contribution of the two host populations. In particular, an A#-like detector network with $\mathcal{O}(10^3)$ dark sirens may be able to exclude scenarios in which the host population traces only one of the two weighting prescriptions. Dark-siren analyses may therefore provide robust cosmological measurements and new information about how merging compact binaries trace the galaxy population.

papers.title: Benefit-Targeted Routing and Bounded Revision for LLM-Based Evidence Screening in Manufacturing Supplier Discovery
papers.abstract: An evidence-review system must allocate additional model judgments and control their use. We study these software decisions on 6,164 frozen manufacturing source-task pairs. Benefit-targeted routing learns recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement. On the original 300-case test, 60 consultations yield 202/231 agreements with two human references versus 189/218 for a logistic-risk router. An additional 300 cases were independently annotated twice using equal frozen evidence. Without retraining the historical policies, the corresponding counts are 164/190 versus 163/193; the differences do not resolve an advantage. Strict scalar-Ridge controls share preprocessing, regularization and fitting, and remain inconclusive. Quotation and requested-state replacement gates retain rejected cases and budget costs; their joint gate rejects one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes. Evidence ablations, fusion and bounded updates supply further controls. A completed 200-pair identity audit yields 97.45 percent weighted merge precision after eight author adjudications. This audits a provisional map, while prospective company-disjoint performance remains untested.

papers.title: Terao's freeness conjecture for arrangements of 15 and 16 lines
papers.abstract: We prove that Terao's freeness conjecture holds for arrangements of 15 and of 16 lines in the complex projective plane. Together with the theorem of Barakat and Kühne for at most 14 hyperplanes, this shows that freeness of a central arrangement of at most 16 planes in $\mathbb{C}^3$ is determined by its intersection lattice. The proof has a theoretical and a computational part. Combining published combinatorial criteria for freeness (due to Abe, Dimca, Dimca-Kühne-Pokora and Yoshinaga) with Bojanowski's Hirzebruch-type inequality and an elementary counting identity, we show that a counterexample would have exponents $(6,8)$ or $(7,7)$ for 15 lines and $(7,8)$ for 16 lines, and an intersection lattice subject to strong numerical constraints. We then enumerate all 22,544,280 simple rank 3 matroids satisfying these constraints, up to isomorphism, and determine the complex realization space of each of them exactly over $\mathbb{Q}$. Exactly eleven of them are realizable over $\mathbb{C}$, and on each of these the freeness of the realizations is constant. As a by-product we classify the free arrangements of 15 and 16 lines that are not divisionally free, have maximal multiplicity smaller than the smaller nontrivial exponent, and have at least four intersection points on every line.

papers.title: AeroIntent: A Synchronized Multimodal Benchmark for UAV Mission Intent Recognition
papers.abstract: Reliable recognition of mission-level UAV intent from multimodal observations is essential for low-altitude airspace surveillance and security. Existing multimodal UAV datasets primarily support detection, tracking, and localization, leaving limited support for evaluating mission-intent recognition across held-out trajectory programs and incomplete radar histories. We introduce AeroIntent, a simulation-based benchmark comprising 990 synchronized multimodal sequences generated by 22 trajectory programs across five mission intents. The benchmark provides radar, RGB, infrared, and depth observations, together with program-disjoint, radar-gap, and observation-prefix evaluation protocols. Building on this benchmark, we propose AeroMIR, a structured Multimodal Intent Reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, derived behavioral features, selected visual evidence, and task knowledge for candidate-based UAV intent recognition. Under a strict program-disjoint protocol evaluating unseen tactical realizations, AeroMIR achieves a mean accuracy of 71.56% and a mean Macro-F1 of 69.84% across three seeds, outperforming the strongest trajectory-only baseline by 7.79 Macro-F1 points and a conventional radar-RGB late-fusion baseline by 19.32 points. AeroMIR also demonstrates strong performance under controlled radar gaps and early intent recognition settings. AeroIntent and AeroMIR provide a reproducible foundation for multimodal UAV intent recognition. The benchmark is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AeroIntent

papers.title: Where to weight? Estimating population causal effects with weighted double score matching in complex surveys
papers.abstract: Double score matching is an emerging method for causal inference that combines propensity and prognostic scores to achieve dimension reduction and model robustness. However, when the observational data are drawn from a complex survey, the existing literature does not provide sufficient guidance on the proper use of survey weights in matching strategies for population-level causal inference. We develop weighted double score matching (WDSM) that provides a unified framework for incorporating survey weights throughout the score estimation, matching, and outcome analysis under both retrospective (informative) and prospective (non-informative) sampling designs. We establish asymptotic normality of the resultant effect estimates under both known and estimated scores and develop a linearization-based bootstrap procedure for variance estimation that preserves the survey-weighted matching structure. Simulation studies show that WDSM substantially reduces bias relative to unweighted matching when either the propensity score model or the prognostic score models are correctly specified. Under correct specification, WDSM also improves efficiency and confidence interval coverage relative to survey-weighted propensity score matching, with particularly pronounced gains under poor overlap. Applications to early marijuana use and mental health in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health and to sleep duration and glycemic control in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey illustrate the practical value of WDSM for population-level inference. We conclude with a discussion of our findings and provide practical guidance on incorporating survey weights into matching-based analyses of observational data.

papers.title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

papers.title: Distributed Algorithm for Linear Least Squares Problems via Iteratively Preconditioning by Successive Over-Relaxation
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on a novel distributed optimization algorithm for solving multi-agent linear least squares problems within a server-agent framework. Distributed methods are particularly suited to large-scale systems. The computational tasks can be partitioned across agents, while local data of one agent remain inaccessible to others. The proposed approach employs an iterative preconditioning scheme with the successive over-relaxation technique, leading to a substantial reduction of the number of iterations required for convergence, which presents a critical advantage where server-agent communication is costly. Theoretical convergence proof of the proposed algorithm is presented. Finally, benchmark problems are tested to demonstrate the performance comparison of the proposed approach over several prominent distributed methods.

papers.title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
papers.abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.

papers.title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.

papers.title: Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits over Quantum Networks
papers.abstract: Emerging quantum networks enable distributed quantum computing (DQC) by interconnecting modest, noisy quantum processors. However, practical deployments face tight memory budgets, probabilistic entanglement generation, and decoherence, all while serving multiple users. In realistic settings -- cloud execution, iterative/interactive workloads and concurrent jobs -- circuits do not arrive in a single batch but as a stream. This creates a fundamentally online problem: the system must react to stochastic arrivals, balance latency and throughput, and remain stable under varying loads without foresight of future jobs. We study Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits (OS-DQC) and formalize the online scheduling problem for quantum networks: circuits arrive over time and must be executed without knowledge of future arrivals. At each event time (arrival or completion), the system decides which waiting circuits to launch and how to place their qubits, while accounting for congestion from in-flight circuits and constraints due to finite memories and decoherence. The objective is to minimize the mean completion time and makespan under these physical and resource constraints.

papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.

papers.title: DeltaTrace: Efficient Signed Attribution for Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: We study how words in the context support or oppose a language model's response and present DeltaTrace, a novel attribution framework that explains the effect of input tokens on a fixed model response. DeltaTrace measures how the response's log-probability changes when the context tokens being explained are masked. To distribute this difference among source tokens, it constructs operator-specific local rules for finite changes and composes them backward through the computational graph using effective secant slopes. Each token is assigned a signed attribution as the inner product of its embedding displacement and the corresponding backward-propagated slope. Local conservation makes these contributions sum to the measured score difference and preserves their meaning when aggregated over sentences or passages. DeltaTrace supports both attention and linear-attention models, with auxiliary memory growing linearly with sequence length at fixed model dimensions and chunk size. On the evaluated attention model, DeltaTrace achieves the lowest deletion-faithfulness scores (RISE and MAS) on most retrieval and reasoning tasks and the highest needle-in-a-haystack Recall, exceeding FlashTrace by 5.67-24.33 percentage points. On the evaluated hybrid attention and linear-attention model, DeltaTrace lowers RISE on 9 tasks and MAS on 12 relative to FlashTrace.

papers.title: Non-planar contact structures with Calabi-Yau Fillings and topological quantum computation
papers.abstract: This paper is a non-planar counterpart of the author's earlier work on planar contact structures and topological quantum computation. On a planar page every branch point is paired by a liftable arc, and the pairing matches the Ising representation exactly, in that fixing the channels of the pairs already fixes the state. Here the page has genus g and connected binding, presented as a simple degree-three cover of the disk. Every maximal system of disjoint liftable arcs then has exactly g members and leaves two branch points unused, and the half-twist interchanging the two points is not liftable, although its cube is and lifts to the identity. Ising fusion does not see that leftover pair, determining its channel from the other g and acting there only by scalars, whereas Fibonacci fusion can leave the channel undetermined. The powers of the cube then act by ten distinct relative phases on a single joint eigenspace, while the Calabi-Yau Stein filling stays fixed. An integral residue criterion supplies the Calabi-Yau test, a factorization localized on a contact connected sum is automatically Calabi-Yau, and, unlike in the planar case, a Calabi-Yau factorization need not be the shortest.

papers.title: Cling: Supporting Cross-Page Coordination with Human-Directed, In-Situ, and Small-Step Automation
papers.abstract: Web-based information work spans independently developed pages, with goals and coordination needs often emerging through browsing. Manual coordination requires repeated low-level actions, yet explicitly specifying operations for automation can interrupt engagement with information that shapes users' next steps. Our approach constructs reusable, schema-based page representations and identifies coordination actions through correspondences across schemas. We instantiate this approach in Cling, which surfaces coordination opportunities in situ for users to select, configure, and execute incrementally while directing the broader task. A technical evaluation demonstrates accurate identification of useful opportunities across diverse domains. A 12-participant study found that Cling reduced task durations by more than half compared with both manual interaction and an end-to-end AI agent, while requiring 61% fewer clicks and 80% fewer tab switches than manual interaction. Its small-step automation supported control and verification as actions unfolded, while accommodating intent as it emerged and evolved through information encountered on the page.

papers.title: Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.

papers.title: Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.

papers.title: Thermodynamics of two-flavor isospin-asymmetric superfluid quark matter at next-to-leading order
papers.abstract: We study quark matter at high isospin asymmetry in the limit of vanishing baryon density, a state of matter governed by the condensation of charged pions. In the weak-coupling limit, this state of matter can be reliably described by conventional perturbative methods where a trivial ground state is assumed. However, since the condensate of charged pions generates a gap in the excitation spectrum of the quarks with a non-perturbative dependence on the strong coupling, corrections to the results from conventional perturbative methods arise. This situation is very reminiscent of the one encountered in isospin-symmetric quark matter at high baryon densities which is expected to be a color superconductor. In the present work, we calculate the thermodynamic properties of superfluid quark matter at high isospin asymmetry, zero temperature, and zero baryon density at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the coupling in the presence of a finite gap. We work in the limit of two massless quark flavors and further assume that the gap is small compared to the isospin chemical potential. Similar to the situation in color-superconducting quark matter at high baryon densities, we find that the gap-induced corrections lead to an increase of the pressure and the speed of sound above their values obtained for non-superfluid quark matter. Notably, starting from asymptotically high isospin asymmetries, these corrections lead to a systematic change of the slope of the speed of sound when the isospin asymmetry is decreased. We compare our results with recent lattice QCD and Dyson-Schwinger equation studies and find good agreement in the regimes where these methods are applicable.

papers.title: Two-step nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by quivers and geometric structures
papers.abstract: In the study of geometric structures on nilmanifolds, two-step nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by graphs play an important role. Recently, additional examples of nilpotent Lie algebras have been constructed from finite quivers without cycles. These latter examples can have arbitrarily high degrees of nilpotency, and admit Riemannian Ricci soliton metrics. In this paper, we study nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by finite quivers without cycles that are two-step nilpotent, and we prove that they can also be obtained by graphs. Using this relationship, we demonstrate that every two-step nilpotent Lie algebra obtained by a finite quiver without cycles admits a pseudo-Riemannian Ricci-flat metric. Additionally, we also classify these nilpotent Lie algebras that admit symplectic structures.

papers.title: Phase transitions of the antiferromagnetic $J_1$-$J_2$-$J_3$ Ising model on the cubic lattice
papers.abstract: Motivated by the conflicting findings in prior studies regarding the nature of the phase transition for the three-dimensional antiferromagnetic $J_1$-$J_2$-$J_3$ Ising model on the cubic lattice with $J_1 = J_2 = J_3 = 1.0$, in this study we conduct a detailed investigation of this model using both Monte Carlo simulations and neural networks (NN). Here $J_1$ and $J_2$ are the intralayer nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor couplings, respectively, and $J_3$ is the nearest-neighbor interlayer interaction. By investigating the data obtained from much larger lattices than those used in previous studies, we find that the phase transition for $J_1 = J_2 = J_3 = 1.0$ is second order without any ambiguity. Hence we bring a resolution to this debate. Apart from $J_1 = J_2 = J_3 = 1.0$, we study the critical phenomenon associated with $J_2/J_1 = 4/7$ and $J_3 = J_1 = 1.0$ as well. In addition, by employing a dedicated training and testing strategy, our NN computation not only is much more efficient than those utilizing the standard procedures commonly used in the literature, but also requires only a per-mille fraction of the storage capacity needed by a conventional NN calculation when a large linear system size $L$ is considered. The method employed here provides an extremely resource-efficient route for applying NN techniques to study the critical behaviors of higher-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Quantum computing for plasma physics in magnetic-confinement fusion
papers.abstract: Plasma simulations for magnetic-confinement fusion (MCF) involve high-dimensional kinetic dynamics, strong nonlinear coupling, complex geometries, and multiscale spatiotemporal behavior, imposing severe computational bottlenecks. While quantum computing offers a potential alternative for accelerating plasma simulation problems, its practical advantage for fusion research has not yet been demonstrated. We review existing quantum computing studies across kinetic dynamics, wave interactions, equilibrium, and macroscopic stability, evaluating their hardware implementations and operational bottlenecks. Current studies remain largely restricted to linearized equations, reduced models, or isolated computational subroutines, leaving a substantial gap from realistic fusion simulations. We summarize key problem characteristics, including high dimensionality, structured dynamics, and measurement requirements, under which plasma applications are most likely to yield a quantum advantage. Guided by these considerations, we highlight potential approaches and present a roadmap toward practical quantum advantage of simulating plasma in MCF.

papers.title: Extremal arborescences in graph orientations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the extremal number of arborescences over orientations of a fixed graph. We prove that every alternating orientation of a plane Eulerian multigraph minimizes the rooted arborescence count among its Eulerian orientations. We also prove that every tournament of odd order maximizing the total number of arborescences is regular, and hence Eulerian. These results resolve Conjectures 5.1 and 5.4 of Bandekar et al. We further establish upper bounds for arborescence counts in orientations of complete bipartite graphs and characterize the orientations attaining them.

papers.title: Rethinking Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Few-Shot Learning Perspective on Overfitting Prevention
papers.abstract: Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for AR/VR and real-time communication applications, yet remains challenging when reconstructing 3D scenes from limited viewpoints. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels in dense-view scenarios, it suffers from overfitting and geometry degradation under sparse inputs. Current approaches often tackle these problems from a local perspective, addressing either data quality or training regularization individually, lacking a unified and interpretable framework for systematic improvement. We introduce a new perspective that reframes sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning viewpoint, treating each Gaussian primitive as a neuron and leveraging deep learning regularization techniques. Under this unified framework, our approach generates more effective supervision from scarce observations through two strategies: (1) data-related supervision enrichment via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization; and (2) training-time regularization via motion-aware dropout and early stopping, which suppress overfitting while preserving dynamic-scene stability. Extensive experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward baselines. Our system won first place in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 challenge.

papers.title: A double-logarithmic lifespan bound for axisymmetric Euler equations with a small initial swirl
papers.abstract: We study the axisymmetric incompressible Euler equations in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with a small initial swirl. Fix $s>7/2$, and let $\boldsymbol{v}_0\in H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)$ be axisymmetric and divergence-free. If $\varepsilon=\|{\nabla\times(v_{0,θ}\boldsymbol{e}_θ)}\|_{L^\infty}$ is sufficiently small, then the lifespan $T_*$ of the corresponding $H^s$ solution satisfies $$ T_{*}\geq\frac{C_s}{1+\|{\boldsymbol{v}_0}\|_{H^s}} \left[ \log\log (\varepsilon^{-1}) \right]^{3/7}\,. $$ This removes the assumption by Danchin (Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 141:1979-1993, 2013) that the domain must be distant from the axis of symmetry. Moreover, even for $\boldsymbol{v}_0\in H^3$, our result improves the fourfold iterated-logarithmic lower bound for the lifespan obtained by Li and Zhou (Z. Angew. Math. Phys. 75:219, 2024) to a threefold iterated-logarithmic bound.

papers.title: Global regularity and sharp decay rates for the one-dimensional hypo-viscous compressible Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the global regularity of the one-dimensional hypo-viscous compressible Navier--Stokes equations in the critical Besov spaces, where the initial data are close to the constant equilibrium state. We introduce an effective velocity, constructed as a combination of the density and the velocity, which is used to capture the high-frequency behavior of $a$. By performing elaborate high-frequency and low-frequency estimates together with a bootstrap argument, we obtain global existence for $\frac{1}{2}\leβ<1$. In particular, when $\frac{1}{2}\leβ<\frac{3}{4}$, we also prove the uniqueness of solutions. Furthermore, under an additional low-frequency assumption, we establish the optimal time decay rates.

papers.title: Kähler-Finsler rigidity of the Kobayashi metric and the Kähler base of weakly Kähler-Finsler metrics
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a rigidity theorem: for every balanced, smooth, bounded pseudoconvex domain, its Kobayashi metric is a smooth, strongly pseudoconvex, Kähler-Finsler metric restricted on a neighborhood of the origin if and only if the domain is a Hermitian ellipsoid, biholomorphic to the unit ball. Thus for any balanced, smooth, bounded, strictly convex, and strongly pseudoconvex domain that is not biholomorphic to the unit ball, its Kobayashi metric is a non-Kähler-Finsler, weakly Kähler-Finsler metric. We also prove that the base manifold of every weak Kähler-Finsler metric is Kähler.

papers.title: On the group of automorphisms of the escaping sets of Hénon maps
papers.abstract: In this article, we provide an explicit description of $\operatorname{Aut}_1(I_H^+)$, the group of automorphisms of the escaping set $I_H^+$ of a Hénon map that induce the identity on its fundamental group. More precisely, for a Hénon map $H(x,y)=(y,p(y)-δx),$ where $p$ is a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ and $δ\neq 0$, we show that $\operatorname{Aut}_1(I_H^+)$ is completely determined by the degree and the coefficients of $p$. Thus, the automorphism group of the escaping set, subject to the prescribed topological constraint, can be explicitly characterized in terms of the underlying Hénon map.

papers.title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification
papers.abstract: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.

papers.title: Motor compound fault diagnosis using an attention-based cross-talk architecture
papers.abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.

papers.title: Euclid Bypass end-to-end simulations for spectroscopic galaxy clustering performance assessment
papers.abstract: We present a simulation framework for Euclid galaxy clustering measurements that reproduces the essential behaviour of the spectroscopic reduction chain, bypassing the computation required by full pixel-level simulations. The framework comprises two complementary tools, FastSpec, which simulates 1-dimensional slitless spectra with a simplified instrument and noise model, and Pypelid, which computes detection probabilities on input catalogues, accounting for the survey dithering sequence and spatially varying noise. We develop calibrated prescriptions for the survey selection function, redshift errors, and redshift interloper populations. Applied to the Euclid Wide Survey, the baseline selection yields a redshift purity of 74% and a sample completeness of 45%, which improves with the use of Euclid photometric colours. The redshift error distribution is found to have a Gaussian core of width $σ_z = 9.4 \times 10^{-4}$, with no significant trend over $0.9 < z < 1.8$. Emission lines [OIII]5008 and [SIII]9530 misidentified as H$α$ contribute a few to ten per cent depending on redshift, while catastrophic redshift measurement failures dominate at low signal-to-noise ratio. Simulating the Data Release 1 footprint, we find that complex survey selection effects can be corrected with a forward-modelled random catalogue, recovering the monopole and quadrupole of the galaxy 2-point correlation function. The simplified noise model does not include residual contamination from overlapping spectra, or other artefacts seen in early Euclid data; this will be revisited with DR1 data. The framework provides an efficient route for characterising the Euclid spectroscopic selection function at the precision required for galaxy clustering science, and is the basis for systematic error assessments in Euclid galaxy clustering analyses.

papers.title: How Quantum Is Light? Concepts, Measures, and Applications of Optical Quantumness
papers.abstract: Quantum states are ultimately responsible for numerous counterintuitive phenomena that defy classical intuition. As the development of quantum technologies accelerates, our ability to harness these quantum resources becomes essential. This review addresses a fundamental question. How do we quantify the quantumness of a state, and which specific traits distinguish it from its classical counterparts? We examine quantumness through both theoretical and operational lenses, providing a clear framework for state characterization. Ultimately, we demonstrate that certifying quantumness is not just a theoretical exercise. It is a practical necessity for identifying, and realizing quantum advantage in real-world applications.

papers.title: A high-Galactic-altitude scattering screen: scintillation from Globular Cluster pulsar M53A
papers.abstract: While known interstellar scattering screens are largely confined to the Galactic disk, the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the deep Galactic halo have remained unexplored. Using observations from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectra of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A). Under the 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models considered here, the inferred scintillation screen distances are $12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8}$\,kpc, respectively. These model-dependent estimates correspond to Galactic heights of $12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7}$\,kpc, placing the candidate screen among the highest-altitude scattering structures inferred to date. The strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry suggests substantial electron-density inhomogeneity within the screen. We speculate that this screen is associated with small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble. These results support the presence of discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep within the Galactic halo, far beyond the regions where localized stellar feedback is typically concentrated, and highlight pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM.

papers.title: When Should AI Chime In? Benchmarking Timely Contribution of Proactive Agents in Multi-Party Chat
papers.abstract: Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.

papers.title: Budgeted Attack Scheduling for LLM Red-Teaming: The Roles of Static Priors, Semantic Guidance, and Online Feedback
papers.abstract: As jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) become increasingly diverse, red-teaming has come to rely on large libraries of jailbreak prompts and attack strategies to evaluate the robustness of victim models and their defense settings. However, attack effectiveness is highly condition-dependent: an attack that succeeds under one victim-defense setting may fail under another, while exhaustively evaluating the full attack library for each setting incurs substantial token and monetary costs. This motivates studying how jailbreak attacks should be prioritized under a limited attempt budget for efficient robustness evaluation. In this work, we formalize this problem as budgeted attack scheduling over a fixed attack library and investigate three complementary signals under a fixed victim-defense condition: (1) static historical attack success rate (ASR) priors; (2) semantic guidance from LLMs; and (3) online feedback from earlier queries. Building on these signals, we design four scheduling strategies and evaluate them across three victim models and three defense settings on GPT-5.2. Extensive experiments clearly characterize the conditions under which each signal is most effective. Historical ASR provides a strong initialization, but its reliability degrades under defense-induced distribution shifts. Semantic guidance consistently improves or matches static prior-based scheduling in the cold-start regime, while online feedback becomes particularly valuable when transferred priors become stale. Semantic guidance and online feedback can also partially compensate for missing historical priors. Taken together, these findings characterize budgeted red-teaming as an attack scheduling problem in which historical priors, semantic guidance, and online feedback play complementary roles.

papers.title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
papers.abstract: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and correlation evaluation make analyses across recordings and parameter settings computationally expensive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation that expresses the matching objective as additive interval contributions and computes t-distance from reusable correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction, sequential local refinement, and active-block reuse complement CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton execution paths. Across seven controlled workloads with two input realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1,730. All 168 optimized executions reproduce complete reference boundary histories and selected state counts, with a maximum absolute t-distance difference of $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four publicly supplied BBBD EEG analysis matrices provide complementary cross-backend validation. A naturalistic fMRI application segments 4,230 angular-gyrus voxels in a group response and 16 participants; the 17 CPU fits total 213.10 seconds. Mean pairwise boundary alignment exceeds a circular-shift baseline, illustrating cohort-level use of the saved segmentations. Versioned results, recording-level parallelism, and optional low-memory execution support varied analysis scales. HP-GSBS connects an explicit mathematical reformulation of repeated computation to efficient and reproducible neural-state analysis.

papers.title: SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SWE) benchmarks are the primary way to measure the capabilities of coding agents: an agent is placed in a code repository or machine environment, given a request, and judged by hidden tests. These benchmarks almost always start the agent from a clean state that contains no earlier work on the task. In practice, however, agents often continue work that a developer or another agent has already done and reported as complete, with no indication of what remains incorrect or missing. We introduce SWE-Residual, a benchmark for Starting-State Robustness: the ability to maintain performance on a task when the starting state already contains earlier work on that task. SWE-Residual contains 198 Residual States drawn from 111 tasks in DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench, where the earlier work modifies a code repository or a whole machine environment. Each Residual State is the state a predecessor agent left behind after submitting its work as complete, although the hidden tests still fail. The evaluated agent receives only the original request and this state, without the predecessor's trajectory or any sign that the attempt failed; because the request and hidden tests are unchanged, the starting state is the only difference from the source benchmark. Across five frontier agents, success drops by 20.6--53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6--34.9 points on Terminal-Bench relative to a Clean Start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. Failed continuations show a pattern we call acceptance bias: agents treat the inherited work as the definition of what remains to be done instead of checking it against the request. On DeepSWE, in 58.9--88.2% of failed runs, they submit with exactly the same tests failing, although they pass most of these tests from a Clean Start. SWE-Residual thus exposes a capability gap that clean-start evaluation does not capture.

papers.title: A characterization of Griffiths semipositivity by top-degree optimal $\bar \partial$-estimates
papers.abstract: We prove that a singular Hermitian metric $h$ on a vector bundle agrees almost everywhere with a Griffiths semipositive metric if its dual metric $h^*$ is locally integrable and the $\bar \partial$-equation admits solutions with optimal $L^2$-estimates for $(n,n)$-forms, where $n$ is the dimension of the base manifold. In particular, under this integrability assumption, Nakano semipositivity in the sense of optimal estimates implies Griffiths semipositivity.

papers.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.

papers.title: Exact extremizers for $\ell_p$-judicious bisections of triangle-free graphs
papers.abstract: Balogh, Clemen and Lidický asked how large the minimum $\ell_p$-norm of the internal-edge counts over balanced partitions of an $n$-vertex triangle-free graph can be. For each fixed $2<p<\infty$ and all sufficiently large even $n$, we determine this value exactly for bisections and characterize all extremal graphs. They are precisely the complete bipartite graphs $K_{a,n-a}$ for which $a\le n/2$ maximizes an explicit integer objective. All maximizing values of $a$ lie in an interval of length bounded in terms of $p$ alone. We also prove quantitative stability for the same range of $p$ and $n$: for sufficiently small $δ\ge 0$, every $n$-vertex triangle-free graph with bisection value at least the asymptotic optimum minus $δn^2$ is within $O_p(δn^2+n)$ edge edits of a complete bipartite graph with the optimal limiting class ratio.

papers.title: On nilpotent Lie algebras arising from parabolic subalgebras and quivers --- three-step cases
papers.abstract: Nilpotent Lie groups are important subjects for studying spacial left-invariant geometric structures. However, nilpotent Lie groups are impossible to classify, and even the two-step case has not been classified. There are several classes of examples of nilpotent Lie algebras that arise with higher nilpotency steps. In this paper, we focus on two of these methods. The first one is the nilpotent parts of parabolic subalgebras of semisimple Lie algebras. The second one is the nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by quivers. We list and compare nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by these two methods that are three-step and of dimension at most 10.

papers.title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
papers.abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.

papers.title: Invitation to torso parameters of annotated graphs
papers.abstract: An annotated graph is a pair $(G,S)$, where $G$ is a graph and $S$ is a subset of vertices of $G$. We present a unified approach for definitions of annotated versions of classical graph parameters such as treewidth, pathwidth, treedepth, etc. A generic way to incorporate a distinguished set of vertices into a graph parameter is via torsos. Given a graph $G$ and a subset $S'\subseteq V(G)$, we define $\mathrm{torso}_G(S')$ to be the graph with vertex set $S'$ in which distinct vertices $u,v\in S'$ are adjacent if and only if there exists a $u$-$v$ path in $G$ whose internal vertices lie outside $S'$. Now let $\mathrm{p}$ be any graph parameter. For an annotated graph $(G,S)$, we define the torso $\mathrm{p}$ of $(G,S)$ by \[\mathrm{p}(G,S) = \min\{\mathrm{p}(\mathrm{torso}_G(S')) \mid S \subset S' \subset V(G)\}.\] For a minor-closed class of annotated graphs $\mathcal{C}$, we discuss equivalent conditions for $\mathrm{p}(G,S)$ bounded for all $(G,S)\in\mathcal{C}$ in terms of annotated graphs excluded in $\mathcal{C}$. In many cases, we collect known results from the literature. We include two new arguments for $\mathrm{p}$ being the $2$-treedepth and the feedback vertex number. Among other statements, we also include a variant of the Erdős-Pósa property for annotated cycles. We propose some new research directions.

papers.title: An Analysis of Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Co-evolution for Edge Classification on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Dynamic edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks, community forums, and news-derived knowledge graphs, requires high quality, adaptive semantic representations in the context of network evolution. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically initialize text feature vectors with pretrained language models and hold them static during training to preserve their semantic structure, forgoing the potential benefits of allowing them to co-evolve with network topology. In this work, we investigate the effects of enabling such co-evolution with a unified text-graph alignment framework that integrates a lightweight Transformer adapter to update token-level text representations via spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective. To prevent detrimental semantic distortion, a language model maintenance objective anchors the evolving text embeddings to their original semantic structure. Evaluations on the Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark demonstrate that this anchored text-graph co-evolution consistently improves upon the edge classification performance of frozen-text baselines across diverse Web-related domains. Representational analyses reveal that the framework reduces anisotropy, improving the linear separability of text embeddings, and effectively encodes structural and temporal information into the semantic space. A computational efficiency analysis confirms that this beneficial semantic and spatio-temporal co-evolution is achieved without incurring the prohibitive computational overhead typical of end-to-end joint training.

papers.title: The $(n-2)$-linear restriction estimate in $\mathbb R^n$
papers.abstract: We present a proof for the $(n-2)$-linear extension estimate for curved surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\ge5$, at the local product exponent $2(n-1)/(n-2)^2$, with an arbitrarily small power loss. The hypotheses are transversality of the normals and nondegeneracy of the compressed shape operators on their common two-dimensional orthogonal complement. The argument combines polynomial partitioning, a descent through algebraic varieties, localized multilinear restriction, and positive packet-energy estimates.

papers.title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.

papers.title: Constraints on the Cosmic Expansion Rate Using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey and the Fifth Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide a calibration-free measure of distances, offering important input on the long-standing tension between early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant ($H_0$). In the absence of an electromagnetic counterpart, the dark siren method can be employed to statistically correlate a gravitational wave event's localization with a galaxy catalog of potential hosts. We present a measurement of the Hubble constant using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey Data Release 3 and the fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog. Applying the dark siren method to a large, photometrically heterogeneous footprint required revised catalog-construction choices: a faint apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r<20$) to control known photometric-redshift bias, a bright apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r>15.5$) to exclude saturated sources, implementation of an evolving luminosity function parameterization, and de-biasing survey regions based on survey depth and photometric redshift precision. With these choices applied to DELVE, we obtain $H_0= 67.4^{+13.0}_{-11.2}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ from dark sirens alone, and $H_0= 70.6^{+8.7}_{-7.0}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ when combined with the bright siren GW170817. We test other galaxy catalog configuration choices, and find subdominant influence from photometric band choice and luminosity function parameterization on the final $H_0$ posterior. Our results demonstrate that extending the dark siren method to wider-area, non-uniform galaxy surveys is feasible and provides additional constraining power on $H_0$ relative to the spectral siren method, opening the door for analyses with forthcoming galaxy catalogs from LSST, Euclid, and Roman.

papers.title: Approximation numbers of critical Besov embeddings
papers.abstract: We determine the approximation numbers of critical embeddings between isotropic Besov spaces on nonempty bounded Lipschitz domains in any dimension. For 0 < p_1 < 2 < p_2 <= infinity and s_1 - s_2 = d max{1/p_1, 1 - 1/p_2} > d(1/p_1 - 1/p_2), the approximation numbers have order N^{-1/2}(log(e+N))^Gamma for every 0 < q_1, q_2 <= infinity, with an explicit four-case formula for Gamma. This resolves the strictly compact critical Besov approximation-number problem identified in Vybiral's overview. For q_1 < q_2, the logarithmic exponent depends on the ordering of p_1' and p_2; it can vanish for one pair (p_1,p_2) and remain positive for another with the same fine indices. A row estimate for the approximation error gives lower bounds when the target fine index is below one. Gaussian finite-rank approximations acting on several levels give the sharp upper bounds when Gamma < 1/2. For q_1 < q_2, matching lower bounds for the two strict orderings of the inner indices follow from Malykhin's finite-window estimates and norm comparisons. The results include quasi-Banach indices and the full spaces of bounded coefficient sequences at infinite fine indices.

papers.title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

papers.title: One-Bit Coherent Distributed Radar Detection in Clutter via Velocity-Plane Search: Vanishing Loss and EEC-Calibrated Thresholding
papers.abstract: Coherent distributed radar architectures enhance the detectability of low-reflectivity targets. However, conventional coherent processing generally entails prohibitively large volumes of inter-station data exchange, thereby motivating the adoption of one-bit quantization strategies. In this work, we investigate a clutter-dominated regime in which the interference is driven by a dense ensemble of weak scatterers. We demonstrate that, under these conditions, one-bit quantization can exhibit a vanishing performance loss with respect to ideal high-resolution sampling in terms of detection capability, in contrast to the classical 2 dB performance penalty associated with one-bit detection in white Gaussian noise environments. For unknown target velocity, we reformulate joint velocity-search processing under the effective one-bit model. Maximizing over the velocity plane makes false-alarm calibration an extreme-value problem for a correlated two-dimensional random field, whose maximum is not characterized by its pointwise null distribution alone. We therefore use an expected Euler characteristic approximation to calibrate the search threshold. We obtain analytic expressions for a separable two-station geometry and use constrained coefficient fitting for larger networks. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate negligible quantization loss in the clutter-dominated setting and conservative false-alarm calibration under the tested Gaussian slow-time model.

papers.title: Entanglement-enhanced Ramsey spectroscopy of broadband signals
